Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems

Hanrui Zhang Affiliation: Chinese University of Hong Kong Email: hanrui@cse.cuhk.edu.hk
Abstract

We study online selection problems subject to arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, under different arrival orders, with different distributional assumptions. We establish the following bounds: (1) Θ⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)\Theta(\log^{2}n/\log\log n) for the standard (adversarial-order) prophet problem, (2) Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) for the (Bayesian, random-order) prophet secretary problem, and by extension, for the standard (prior-free, random-order) secretary problem, and (3) O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n) for the free-order prophet problem. Together with complementary bounds established in prior work, these results pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all these variants of prophet and secretary problems subject to downward-closed constraints. Our results refine and reinforce the big-decisions-first principle by Rubinstein and Singla [2026], establishing a superconstant separation between the random-order and free-order models.

1 Introduction

Prophet and secretary problems are among the most natural and well studied online selection problems. There are nn items arriving online, each with a value to be revealed upon arrival. After observing the value, the algorithm must irrevocably make a decision to either accept or reject the item. Accepted items are constrained: together, they must form a feasible set as specified by a given set system. The reward collected by the algorithm is the total value of the accepted items, which is to be compared against the prophet benchmark, i.e., the maximum total value that an omniscient prophet can collect. In particular, the typical goal is to optimize the competitive ratio, which is the ratio between the expectation of the prophet benchmark, and that of the algorithm’s performance. The set system that specifies feasibility deserves particular attention, since how rich it can be largely determines the difficulty of the problem. In this paper, we consider fully general systems that are downward-closed.

Variants of the problem are induced by different arrival orders and distributional assumptions. The following variants tend to receive the most attention:

  • •

    The standard prophet problem: the items arrive in an adversarial order, and the algorithm knows the prior distributions of the items’ (independent) values.

  • •

    The standard secretary problem: the items arrive in a uniformly random order, with no prior information about the values given to the algorithm.

  • •

    The prophet secretary problem: the items arrive in a uniformly random order, and the algorithm also knows the prior distributions of the values.

  • •

    The free-order prophet problem: the algorithm knows the prior distributions of the values, and even gets to choose an order of arrival.

The free-order prophet problem is no harder than the prophet secretary problem, which is no harder than both the standard prophet problem and the standard secretary problem.

With downward-closed feasibility systems, the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all the above variants remained open, although the largest gap was already as small as O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)2)O((\log\log n)^{2}). We close all these gaps. In particular, we establish the following main results:

  • •

    Lower bounds:

    • –

      Ω⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)\Omega(\log^{2}n/\log\log n) for the standard prophet problem.

    • –

      Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) for the prophet secretary problem, which by extension also applies to the standard secretary problem.

  • •

    Upper bounds:

    • –

      O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n) for the standard prophet problem with binary values, which through the blackbox extension argument by Rubinstein (2016) implies O⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)O(\log^{2}n/\log\log n) for the same problem with general values.

    • –

      O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n) for the free-order prophet problem.

For the standard prophet problem, our new bounds match. For all other variants, our new bounds match the existing complementary bounds established in prior work. The prior and new bounds are summarized in Table 1.

Conceptually, these tight bounds refine and reinforce the big-decisions-first principle of Rubinstein and Singla (2026): the free-order problem admits the smallest tight ratio, followed by the random-order problems (where distributional information does not even help asymptotically), followed by the adversarial-order problem. This corresponds to increasingly little freedom for the algorithm to process ‘‘bigger’’ items first.11 1 This is best illustrated in the lower bound constructions, where all items are weighted Bernoulli, and the weight measures how “big” an item is. Rubinstein and Singla (2026) already establish the separation between adversarial-order and random-order models, which is further tightened in this paper. In addition, we establish a smaller but superconstant separation between random-order and free-order models too.

1.1 Technical Overview

1.1.1 Lower Bounds

We first discuss the lower bound constructions, starting with a common structure that unifies both our new lower bounds and the previous almost tight lower bound by Rubinstein and Singla (2026).

A shared structure for lower bounds: layered self-encoding.

Consider the following abstract construction. The entire instance is divided into TT layers (where typically T=Θ⁡(log⁡n)T=\Theta(\log n), generally indexed by tt. We generally construct the prophet benchmark by visiting the layers in the order of 11 to TT. In the adversarial-order model, we (as well as Rubinstein and Singla (2026)) force the algorithm to process the layers in the reverse order of TT to 11. By the big-decisions-first principle, one would naturally expect items in earlier layers to be bigger. In our constructions, all items in a single layer are independently activated with the same probability, and each layer contributes roughly the same amount in expectation to the prophet benchmark. Accordingly, later layers host more items (which are smaller) than earlier layers.

Each layer tt is further divided into dtd_{t} coordinates. These coordinates contain disjoint items, and all items within a single coordinate are mutually exclusive, i.e., a feasible selection can contain at most one item within a single coordinate. Items in each coordinate are indexed by two “symbols”: one from a “message” alphabet ΣM\Sigma_{M}, and one from a “codeword” alphabet ΣC,t\Sigma_{C,t} which can vary across layers (we will explain what messages and codewords are momentarily). So within a coordinate in layer tt, there are |ΣM|⋅|ΣC,t||\Sigma_{M}|\cdot|\Sigma_{C,t}| mutually exclusive items. And layer tt contains dt⋅|ΣM|⋅|ΣC,t|d_{t}\cdot|\Sigma_{M}|\cdot|\Sigma_{C,t}| items in total. We will index items using the tuple (t,i,(mt)i,(ct)i)(t,i,(m_{t})_{i},(c_{t})_{i}), i.e., the item in coordinate ii of layer tt, whose corresponding message symbol and codeword symbol are (mt)i(m_{t})_{i} and (ct)i(c_{t})_{i}. One caveat is that items here might be conceptual: in the adversarial-order construction, we actually replace each conceptual item with a group of identical physical items that are jointly feasible, but each incompatible with any other groups within the same coordinate (so the groups inherit the feasibility of the original conceptual items). Physical items within a group need not be explicitly indexed (at least not in this overview): the groups simply force the same effect in the mutually exclusive groups construction by Babaioff et al. (2007) that forces the algorithm to commit to a group as soon as it takes one physical item in that group. This contributes a factor of Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\log n/\log\log n) in the adversarial-order lower bound. From now on, we will use the term “items” by default, and say “groups” in the adversarial-order construction, where we need to distinguish between groups and physical items.

To describe the feasibility system, we will adopt a self-coding interpretation. Each layer tt carries a message mtm_{t}, whose length is dtd_{t} (so each coordinate of the layer is also a coordinate of the message), i.e., mt∈ΣMdtm_{t}\in\Sigma_{M}^{d_{t}}. Each layer also “inherits” a codeword ctc_{t} whose length is also dtd_{t}, which is conceptually obtained by encoding messages in previous layers m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1} using a public encoder ftf_{t}, i.e., ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)∈ΣC,tdtc_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1})\in\Sigma_{C,t}^{d_{t}}. The encoder is expected to have some kind of error correction property: on two different input sequences of messages, the output codes can only intersect on few coordinates.22 2 Parts of the input messages may be dropped before encoding, in which case differences in the dropped part do not force small intersections. This happens in our prophet secretary construction. This crucial property forces the online algorithm to make commitments that greatly limits its subsequent options — we will get back to this point soon.

Each maximal feasible set is specified by a sequence of messages (m1,…,mT)(m_{1},\dots,m_{T}), one for each layer. Let ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}) for each tt. The corresponding set of items is

{(t,i,(mt)i,(ct)i)∣t∈[T],i∈[dt]}.\{(t,i,(m_{t})_{i},(c_{t})_{i})\mid t\in[T],i\in[d_{t}]\}.

That is, in every layer, we collect the item in each coordinate whose two symbols match the corresponding coordinates of mtm_{t} and ctc_{t}. Each layer tt contributes precisely dtd_{t} conceptual items.

Intuitively, the layered self-encoding structure gives the prophet greater freedom, because in the order of 11 to TT, upon processing each fresh layer, the prophet gets to choose the entire message mtm_{t}. Our constructions make it so that the prophet can extract a constant fraction of the maximum value possible in this layer. The algorithm, on the other hand, is forced to either process items from different layers in a uniformly random order, or from layer TT to layer 11. So the algorithm inevitably faces a dilemma:

  • •

    If the algorithm takes too many items from later (according to the prophet order) layers, it must have already committed to a codeword in some layer tt, because error correction ensures that two different codewords cannot contain too many items in common in one layer. This pins down (a large part of) the messages in previous layers m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}, and by implication also the codewords in all previous layers c1,…,ct−1c_{1},\dots,c_{t-1}. As a result, most (if not all) choices in previous layers are fixed, which forces a loss compared to the flexible prophet benchmark.

  • •

    If the algorithm waits for items in earlier layers and takes only a few items in later layers in the meantime, then it is already missing a lot of value in the process of waiting, which is also a loss compared to the prophet benchmark.

Our new constructions, as well as the earlier construction by Rubinstein and Singla (2026), are based on this intuitive dilemma. They apply different concrete constructions (especially in the encoder ftf_{t}) in response to different arrival orders, and use different accounting arguments to bound the inevitable losses. We discuss them next.

The standard prophet lower bound: a code sensitive to first divergence.

Under the layered self-encoding interpretation, our lower bound construction for the adversarial-order model can be directly compared with that by Rubinstein and Singla (2026). The main differences are twofold: the code being used, and how same-layer hardness is exploited. We first review the construction by Rubinstein and Singla (2026). Roughly speaking, the code used by Rubinstein and Singla (2026) has the following guarantee: for each layer tt, sequences of messages (m1,…,mt)(m_{1},\dots,m_{t}) and (m1′,…,mt′)(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t}^{\prime}), and the corresponding codewords ct=ft​(m1,…,mt)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t}) and ct′=ft​(m1′,…,mt′)c_{t}^{\prime}=f_{t}(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t}^{\prime}),33 3 Rubinstein and Singla (2026) allow the codeword ctc_{t} to depend on mtm_{t} in addition to m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}. Superficially, this goes only slightly beyond the layered self-encoding framework. But it allows their code to enforce same-layer hardness, which is handled by replacing conceptual items with groups of physical items in our construction. This is one of the two key differences that is less relevant to our construction.

  • •

    If mt≠mt′m_{t}\neq m_{t}^{\prime}, then |ct∩ct′|/dt≤1/Θ⁡(T)|c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|/d_{t}\leq 1/\Theta(T).

  • •

    If mτ≠mτ′m_{\tau}\neq m_{\tau}^{\prime} for some τ<t\tau<t, then |ct∩ct′|/dt≤1/Θ⁡(T2)|c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|/d_{t}\leq 1/\Theta(T^{2}).

Here, dtd_{t} is the number of coordinates in layer tt, T=Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)T=\Theta(\log n/\log\log n) is the number of layers in their construction, and |ct∩ct′|=|{i∣(ct)i=(ct′)i}||c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|=|\{i\mid(c_{t})_{i}=(c_{t}^{\prime})_{i}\}| is a (notation-abusing) shorthand for the number of coordinates in which ctc_{t} and ct′c_{t}^{\prime} agree.

To see why this forces a large loss by the online algorithm, imagine its execution from layer TT to layer 11. As soon as the algorithm takes more than Θ⁡(dt/T2)\Theta(d_{t}/T^{2}) items in a layer tt, it has effectively committed to a sequence of message m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1} up to layer t−1t-1, because two different sequences cannot both contain that many items in layer tt. We call this the phase transition. Before the phase transition, the algorithm can only take an O⁡(1/T2)O(1/T^{2}) fraction of items per layer, losing the same factor against the prophet benchmark. In the layer where the transition happens, the algorithm can freely choose up to an O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) fraction of the items taken by the prophet benchmark.44 4 Taking more would commit to the message in the current layer too, which means all future items in the layer are fixed and subject to discounting because of rare activations. These items therefore contribute little value. This is a smaller loss, but it only happens in one layer, so it makes the algorithm better off only by a constant factor. Finally, after the tranisition, the algorithm has committed to a particular sequence of messages, which means the best it can do is to take all items corresponding to that sequence in all remaining layers. The activation probability of each item is set to Θ⁡(1/T2)\Theta(1/T^{2}), which again forces a loss of the same factor.55 5 The construction of Rubinstein and Singla (2026) does not replace conceptual items by groups of physical items. Such replacements would not immediately strengthen their construction since the code in their construction already incorporates same-layer hardness that the replacements are supposed to capture. Tuning the parameters gives T=Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)T=\Theta(\log n/\log\log n), and a lower bound of Ω⁡((log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)2)\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^{2}).

We use a different code that is sensitive to the “first divergence” in a finer way. For each layer tt, different sequences of messages (m1,…,mt−1)(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}) and (m1′,…,mt−1′)(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t-1}^{\prime}), and the corresponding codewords ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}) and ct′=ft​(m1′,…,mt−1′)c_{t}^{\prime}=f_{t}(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t-1}^{\prime}), our code guarantees that |ct∩ct′|=O⁡(dt/⌊t−τ⌋pow22)|c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|=O(d_{t}/\lfloor t-\tau\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}^{2}), where τ<t\tau<t is the smallest index where mτ≠mτ′m_{\tau}\neq m_{\tau}^{\prime}, and ⌊x⌋pow2\lfloor x\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}} is the largest power of 22 that is no larger than xx. Note that this is not a “stronger” code than that of Rubinstein and Singla (2026): in fact, when t−τt-\tau is small, their code guarantees a much smaller overlap between ctc_{t} and ct′c_{t}^{\prime}, which generally helps the lower bound construction. Nonetheless, taking a more global perspective, what really matters is the sum of these overlaps in all layers since the first divergence between two sequences of messages. Assuming the prophet gains 11 per layer, the algorithm’s performance after the first divergence is bounded by (a constant multiple of)

1+2×1/22+4×1/42+8×1/82​⋯=∑j≥02−j=2.1+2\times 1/2^{2}+4\times 1/4^{2}+8\times 1/8^{2}\dots=\sum_{j\geq 0}2^{-j}=2.

In other words, the total gain of the algorithm after the first divergence is only about the prophet’s gain in one layer, which is a loss of a factor Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T), where T=Θ⁡(log⁡n)T=\Theta(\log n) is the number of layers in our construction. In layers smaller than the first divergence,66 6 The first divergence here is retrospective and informal. The actual execution of the algorithm instead progressively limits possible messages, until the sequence of messages up to the layer being processed is entirely fixed. This is what we call the first divergence. the algorithm cannot choose the messages any more, so it suffers the inevitable loss of order Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T).

The above argument only contributes one of two factors in our lower bound. The other factor comes from replacing conceptual items with groups of physical items, each of size Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Theta(\log n/\log\log n). This forces a loss of the same factor on top of the Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T) factor given by the first divergence argument, because the prophet chooses among many independent groups at each coordinate and finds an all-active group with constant probability.77 7 Importantly, this is possible because upon reaching each layer tt, the prophet is free to choose the message mtm_{t} without any constraints. In the construction by Rubinstein and Singla (2026), this choice is coupled with the codeword in the same layer. The algorithm, on the other hand, must commit to a group as soon as it chooses the first physical item in it. Tuning the parameters gives an overall bound of Θ⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)\Theta(\log^{2}n/\log\log n).

The prophet secretary lower bound: nested prefix encoding.

Our construction for the random-order model uses a very different code tailored to the specific arrival order. The code itself is actually simpler and quite standard, except for the part where it neglects parts of the input sequence of messages (m1,…,mt−1)(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}), which we explain first. Suppose the size of the alphabet for messages |ΣM|=2T|\Sigma_{M}|=2^{T}, and every coordinate (mτ)i(m_{\tau})_{i} of a message is represented as a binary string of length TT. For every τ<t\tau<t, the encoder ftf_{t} in layer tt depends only on the first t−τt-\tau bits of each (mτ)i(m_{\tau})_{i}. Taking another perspective, fixing τ\tau and letting tt grow, ftf_{t} encodes a nested sequence of prefixes of each (mτ)i(m_{\tau})_{i} that also grows. Importantly, for two layers t<t′t<t^{\prime}, ftf_{t} encodes a strict subset of the information encoded by ft′f_{t^{\prime}}, so knowing ct′=ft′​(m1,…,mt′−1)c_{t^{\prime}}=f_{t^{\prime}}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t^{\prime}-1}) also uniquely determines ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}).

Restricted to the part of the messages that is actually encoded, the code gives a fairly standard guarantee (provided by, e.g., the Reed-Solomon code): for any layer tt and sequences of messages (m1,…,mt−1)(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}) and (m1′,…,mt−1′)(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t-1}^{\prime}) that differ on the parts actually encoded by ftf_{t}, |ct∩ct′|=O⁡(dt/T)|c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|=O(d_{t}/T), where ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1}) and ct′=ft​(m1′,…,mt−1′)c_{t}^{\prime}=f_{t}(m_{1}^{\prime},\dots,m_{t-1}^{\prime}). In other words, as soon as the algorithm accepts more than Θ⁡(dt/T)\Theta(d_{t}/T) items in a layer tt, the codeword ctc_{t} is uniquely determined, which means:

  • •

    The codeword cτc_{\tau} for any τ<t\tau<t is also uniquely determined.

  • •

    The encoded prefixes of m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\dots,m_{t-1} are also determined.

The second point in particular allows decreasing freedom for smaller layers τ\tau as t−τt-\tau becomes larger. Importantly, we have to achieve the guarantee using an alphabet for the codeword ΣC\Sigma_{C} (we omit tt in the subscript because this alphabet does not depend on tt in this construction) that is as small as possible. This is optimized in the choice of parameters.

Now we discuss the actual lower bound argument. Throughout the execution of the algorithm, we track an index uu, which is the largest layer in which the algorithm has accepted more than Θ⁡(du/T)\Theta(d_{u}/T) items to force a unique codeword in layer uu. Call this the cutoff layer. We divide items accepted by the algorithm into two types:

  • •

    Unconstrained items: the item lies in layer tt, and immediately before the item’s value is revealed, the cutoff layer u<tu<t. In other words, the determined codeword cuc_{u} itself does not constrain the acceptance decision.

  • •

    Constrained ones: the item lies in layer tt, and immediately before the item’s value is revealed, the cutoff layer u≥tu\geq t. In other words, cuc_{u} partially constrains the acceptance decision, because (1) the codeword ctc_{t} in layer tt is already fixed given cuc_{u}, and (2) we have to fix some coordinate of mtm_{t} (a binary string of length TT) to accept the item, which must be consistent with the prefix dictated by cuc_{u}.

Observe that unconstrained items cannot contribute much anyway: the number of such items in layer tt is at most O⁡(dt/T)O(d_{t}/T), whereas the prophet accepts Θ⁡(dt)\Theta(d_{t}) activated items in the same layer in expectation, leaving a gap of Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T).

The constrained ones require more attention. Intuitively, the constrained ones cannot contribute much too: suppose, for simplicity, that the algorithm first accepts only unconstrained items, and after that it transitions into only accepting constrained items. Then, the total value contributed by constrained items cannot be too large. This is because the construction sets the activation probability of each item to 1/2T1/2^{T}, so once the codeword ctc_{t} in a layer tt is fixed, there is, in expectation, precisely 11 item in each coordinate ii that is activated (the prophet of course collects this item whenever it exists). On the other hand, from the algorithm’s perspective, a prefix of length u−tu-t is already fixed, so the algorithm only gets to choose from 2T−u+t2^{T-u+t} items in each coordinate, with an expected gain of at most 2t−u2^{t-u} in the entire layer (2t−u/dt2^{t-u}/d_{t} in expectation in each coordinate, summed over dtd_{t} coordinates). This is true even assuming the algorithm can take all items consistent with the fixed prefix, ignoring other feasibility constraints. Further summing over t≤ut\leq u, this gives us ∑t≤u2t−u=O⁡(1)\sum_{t\leq u}2^{t-u}=O(1), establishing a gap of Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T). The nested prefix encoding is just strong enough to enable this very sum.

In general, the algorithm of course is allowed to interleave the two types of acceptances. This creates additional technical difficulties. To handle them, the key observation is that the cutoff layer uu increases monotonically throughout the execution of the algorithm, and it can strictly increase only TT times. This gives us an easy way to essentially union bound over the possible behavior of the algorithm and preserve the above intuition. We interpret the uniformly random arrival order in the following way: there are TT bins B1,…,BTB_{1},\dots,B_{T}. Each item is first assigned independently to a uniformly random bin, and then each bin is internally permuted uniformly at random. Items in a single bin arrive consecutively, and bins are ordered from 11 to TT.

We relax the algorithm with the following additional power: it observes the entire order of items, including the bin assignments, before items arrive. In addition, we focus on constrained acceptances and ignore unconstrained ones (which are handled separately above), and we make the cutoff layer uu, together with the determined codeword cuc_{u}, something the algorithm can choose freely subject to monotonicity. Initially, u=0u=0. Upon entering a new bin, the algorithm can choose to strictly increase uu any number of times; at each increase, it can even choose the determined codeword cuc_{u} arbitrarily (i.e., it need not be consistent with the algorithm’s previous choices for smaller uu). As soon as the algorithm enters a bin, as well as when an increase of uu happens, the algorithm immediately harvests all items in the current bin in layers t≤ut\leq u that are consistent with cuc_{u}, even if these items are mutually incompatible. The actual value of an item can only be harvested once, even if it appears in two harvests. We call this the harvesting game. Below we argue why it still gives a lower bound of Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T) even with such additional freedom.

We first bound the intersection of the items compatible with a codeword cuc_{u} (call it the menu M⁡(cu)M(c_{u})) and a particular bin BjB_{j}. We do this by examining smaller components of menus, which we call pieces. A piece Pt,i,s,pP_{t,i,s,p} is defined by a layer tt, a coordinate ii, a codeword symbol s∈ΣCs\in\Sigma_{C}, and a prefix p∈{0,1}ℓp\in\{0,1\}^{\ell} of a message symbol of length ℓ≤T\ell\leq T (recall that each message symbol is a binary string of length TT). It contains all items in coordinate ii of layer tt, whose codeword symbol is ss, and whose message symbol has the prefix pp. Every menu is the union of disjoint pieces, and one can show there are O⁡(n)O(n) possible pieces in total. We apply a concentration bound on the size of the intersection between every piece and every bin, followed by a union bound: with high probability, every piece Pt,i,s,pP_{t,i,s,p} intersects every bin BjB_{j} on O⁡(|Pt,i,s,p|/T+T)O(|P_{t,i,s,p}|/T+T) items. The additive O⁡(T)O(T) contributes very little to a menu even aggregated over all pieces. This means essentially the same concentration happens for all menus simultaneously with high probability. We condition on this event (the complementary case happens too rarely and cannot contribute much). The rest of the argument is simple: the algorithm performs O⁡(T)O(T) harvests in total (one entering each bin, and one for each increase of uu), and in each harvest, it collects O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) of the value available in M⁡(cu)M(c_{u}) in expectation, which is O⁡(1/T)O(1/T). The total value harvested is therefore O⁡(1)O(1), creating a gap of Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T).

1.1.2 Upper Bounds

Now we discuss the upper bounds, both of which involve an induction on the moment generating function of the prophet benchmark that connects it to the optimal online algorithm. We first discuss this induction instantiated for binary values, and how it leads to a bound of O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n) irrespective of the arrival order. The proof compares the recurrence satisfied by the optimal online algorithm with a similar recurrence involving the moment generating function of the prophet benchmark. The argument crucially depends on observing (or really, guessing) the right scale of comparison.

The binary values upper bound: a comparison between two recurrences.

Suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is the feasibility system, and XiX_{i} is the Bernoulli random value of each item ii. For any (residual) set system 𝒮\mathcal{S}, let OPT⁡(𝒮)=max⁡∑i∈SS∈𝒮⁡Xi\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{i\in S}X_{i} denote the (random) prophet benchmark on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. OPT=OPT⁡(ℱ)\operatorname{OPT}=\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F}) is the standard prophet benchmark. We define inclusions and exclusions of an item ii in a system 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} including ii 𝒮/i={S∖{i}∣S∈𝒮,i∈S}\mathcal{S}/i=\{S\setminus\{i\}\mid S\in\mathcal{S},i\in S\}.

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} excluding ii 𝒮∖i={S∖{i}∣S∈𝒮}\mathcal{S}\setminus i=\{S\setminus\{i\}\mid S\in\mathcal{S}\}. This is essentially 𝒮\mathcal{S} restricted to all items other than ii.

For a feasible item ii, OPT⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}) satisfies the following recurrence:

OPT⁡(𝒮)=max⁡{OPT⁡(𝒮∖i),Xi+OPT⁡(𝒮/i)}.\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})=\max\{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i),X_{i}+\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}/i)\}.

Based on this recurrence, restricted to binary values, one can show that for any a≥2a\geq 2,

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]≤𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮∖i)]+pi​(a−1)​𝔼​[aOPT⁡(𝒮/i)],\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}]\leq\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)}]+p_{i}(a-1)\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}/i)}],

where pip_{i} is the probability that Xi=1X_{i}=1. We will compare this with a recurrence for the optimal algorithm that has a similar form.

Consider a fixed adversarial order (the proof in fact works for adaptive adversarial orders that depend only on observed values by the algorithm). Let alg⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}) be the expected (onward) value of the optimal online algorithm on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Suppose item ii arrives next. Observe that alg⁡(𝒮∖i)≥alg⁡(𝒮/i)\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)\geq\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}/i). So we have the following simple recurrence:

alg⁡(𝒮)=alg⁡(𝒮∖i)+pi⋅max⁡{0,1+alg⁡(𝒮/i)−alg⁡(𝒮∖i)}.\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S})=\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)+p_{i}\cdot\max\{0,1+\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}/i)-\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)\}. (1)

We will inductively argue that

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]≤exp⁡(O⁡(a+log⁡m)⋅alg⁡(𝒮)),\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}]\leq\exp(O(a+\log m)\cdot\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S})),

where mm is the number of items involved in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, for any a≥2a\geq 2 by comparing the two recurrences. The essence of the entire argument lies in identifying the above bound, which is essentially done by reverse engineering from the conclusion that we need it to lead to: by choosing a=Θ⁡(log⁡n)a=\Theta(\log n) and 𝒮=ℱ\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{F}, this (together with convexity) immediately implies

Θ⁡(log⁡log⁡n)⋅𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(ℱ)]=log⁡(a𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(ℱ)])≤log⁡𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(ℱ)]≤Θ⁡(log⁡n)⋅alg⁡(ℱ),\Theta(\log\log n)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F})]=\log\left(a^{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F})]}\right)\leq\log\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F})}]\leq\Theta(\log n)\cdot\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{F}),

which means

alg⁡(ℱ)≥Θ⁡(log⁡log⁡n/log⁡n)⋅𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(ℱ)].\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{F})\geq\Theta(\log\log n/\log n)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F})].

Coming back to the inductive proof of the bound on the moment generating function, the induction hypothesis gives

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}] ≤𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮∖i)]+pi​(a−1)​𝔼​[aOPT⁡(𝒮/i)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)}]+p_{i}(a-1)\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}/i)}]
≤exp⁡(O⁡(a+log⁡(m−1))⋅alg⁡(𝒮∖i))+pi​(a−1)⋅exp⁡(O⁡(a+log⁡(m−1))⋅alg⁡(𝒮/i)).\displaystyle\leq\exp(O(a+\log(m-1))\cdot\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i))+p_{i}(a-1)\cdot\exp(O(a+\log(m-1))\cdot\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}/i)).

We only need to bound the latter by exp⁡(O⁡(a+log⁡m)⋅alg⁡(𝒮))\exp(O(a+\log m)\cdot\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S})), which can be expanded by Equation 1 to provide a clearer comparison. We identify two complementary cases: when 1+alg⁡(𝒮/i)−alg⁡(𝒮∖i)>1/21+\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}/i)-\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i)>1/2, i.e., when an activated item brings relatively large gain to the algorithm, and when the same quantity is at most 1/21/2. In the two cases, different quantities dominate, which give the desired inequality in both cases. Technical details are omitted. We remark that the proof relies crucially on binary values in several places, and does not appear easily generalizable to unrestricted values. Our upper bound for the free-order model takes a different approach.

The free-order prophet upper bound: approximation by activated exponentials.

The free-order bound has a clean high-level structure: We first identify a special class of variables, namely activated exponentials. An activated exponential variable of scale ss is the product of a Bernoulli variable (the activation), and an exponential variable of mean ss, independent of each other. A similar inductive argument to the one above shows that, when the values of items are activated exponentials, if we visit the items in decreasing order of the scale, then the optimal online algorithm loses only a factor of 22 compared to the prophet benchmark. We will omit a detailed discussion of this part, since it is structurally very similar to the argument demonstrated above.

Now for general variables, we present a reduction to activated exponential variables, which loses a factor of Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Theta(\log n/\log\log n). The argument handles each item ii separately. It constructs Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Theta(\log n/\log\log n) auxiliary random variables Yi,jY_{i,j}, all being activated exponentials. Moreover, a distribution DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i} is specified over these auxiliary random variables. The desired guarantee is item-wise mutual domination within a margin of Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Theta(\log n/\log\log n): each Yi,jY_{i,j} is dominated by XiX_{i} in terms of the reward it generates (more detail to follow), for both the prophet and the online algorithm; all auxiliary variables Yi,jY_{i,j} on average, amplified by a factor of Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Theta(\log n/\log\log n), dominate the original variable XiX_{i}. Additional reductions are omitted here, which cost O⁡(k)O(k) overall. We next discuss how this (combined with the factor-22 argument for activated exponentials) directly leads to the desired bound.

The actual algorithm is the following: for each XiX_{i}, we sample some jij_{i} from DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}, and let sis_{i} be the scale of Yi,jiY_{i,j_{i}}.88 8 The actual construction first normalizes each XiX_{i} such that its mean becomes 11. It then runs this construction, and obtain the true scale by multiplying sis_{i} with the original mean of XiX_{i}. We ignore this for simplicity here. We visit items in decreasing order of sis_{i}, and run the actual optimal online algorithm for XiX_{i} in that order. Abusing notation, let OPT⁡({Xi})\operatorname{OPT}(\{X_{i}\}) and OPT⁡({Yi,ji})\operatorname{OPT}(\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\}) denote the prophet benchmark on the respective variables, and algσ⁡({Xi})\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{X_{i}\}) and algσ⁡({Yi,ji})\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\}) be the optimal algorithm’s (expected) performance fixing a particular order σ\sigma. The above algorithm works because fixing {ji}\{j_{i}\} (and therefore σ\sigma),

algσ⁡({Xi})≥algσ⁡({Yi,ji}),\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{X_{i}\})\geq\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\}),

because of domination of every Yi,jiY_{i,j_{i}} by XiX_{i}. On the other hand, averaging over the choices of {ji}\{j_{i}\} (and therefore σ\sigma), we have

𝔼⁡[algσ⁡({Yi,ji})]≥𝔼⁡[OPT⁡({Yi,ji})/2]≥Ω⁡(log⁡log⁡n/log⁡n)⋅𝔼⁡[OPT⁡({Xi})],\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\})]\geq\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\})/2]\geq\Omega(\log\log n/\log n)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\{X_{i}\})],

because of domination on average of {Xi}\{X_{i}\} by {Yi,ji}\{Y_{i,j_{i}}\} up to a factor of O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n). Putting the two inequalities together, we get

𝔼⁡[algσ⁡({Xi})]≥Ω⁡(log⁡log⁡n/log⁡n)⋅𝔼⁡[OPT⁡({Xi})],\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(\{X_{i}\})]\geq\Omega(\log\log n/\log n)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\{X_{i}\})],

which is the desired bound.

Now we zoom into a single item ii, and consider the construction of Yi,jY_{i,j}. Without loss of generality, suppose 𝔼⁡[Xi]=1\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=1. Then, by standard reductions, the range that matters in a nontrivial way is [1,2​n][1,2n]. We divide this range into k=Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)k=\Theta(\log n/\log\log n) geometric intervals, whose endpoints are 1=x1<x2<⋯<xk1=x_{1}<x_{2}<\dots<x_{k}. In particular, xj+1=k​xjx_{j+1}=kx_{j}, and xk≥2​nx_{k}\geq 2n. We will associate Yi,jY_{i,j} with the interval [xj,xj+1][x_{j},x_{j+1}]. In particular, the contribution of Yi,jY_{i,j} alone (properly weighted and scaled) already dominates XX up to a constant factor on this interval. So, each interval is covered by at least one auxiliary variable.

Our notion of domination is based on the excess function EX​(t)=𝔼⁡[max⁡{X−t,0}]E_{X}(t)=\mathbb{E}[\max\{X-t,0\}] for a random variable XX and a given threshold tt. In particular, we say XX dominates X′X^{\prime} iff EX​(t)≥EX′​(t)E_{X}(t)\geq E_{X^{\prime}}(t) for all t≥0t\geq 0. Both the performance of the optimal online algorithm and the prophet benchmark are monotone under this notion of domination, which enables the reduction to activated exponentials discussed above. Suppose the weight we give Yi,jY_{i,j} is wi,jw_{i,j}. The probability that we sample Yi,jY_{i,j} is wi,j/Wiw_{i,j}/W_{i}, where Wi=∑jwi,jW_{i}=\sum_{j}w_{i,j}. The desired dominations are:

  • •

    For each jj and t≥0t\geq 0: EYi,j​(t)≤EXi​(t)E_{Y_{i,j}}(t)\leq E_{X_{i}}(t), plus some small shift.

  • •

    For each jj and t∈[xj,xj+1)t\in[x_{j},x_{j+1}): (wi,j/W)⋅EO⁡(k)⋅Yi,j​(t)≥EXi−O⁡(k)​(t)(w_{i,j}/W)\cdot E_{O(k)\cdot Y_{i,j}}(t)\geq E_{X_{i}-O(k)}(t).

These guarantees are achieved using a delicate but well motivated construction of both {Yi,j}\{Y_{i,j}\} and {wi,j}\{w_{i,j}\}. Details are omitted here.

1.2 Further Related Work

The classical secretary problem and prophet inequality originate in optimal stopping: a single irrevocable choice is compared with the best choice in hindsight (Dynkin, 1963; Krengel and Sucheston, 1977; Krengel and Sucheston, 1978). Hajiaghayi et al. (2007) observe their connections to auctions and pricing. See (Lucier, 2017) for the economic perspective, (Correa et al., 2019a) for a more focused overview on single-item variants, and (Gupta and Singla, 2021) for more on random-order models. We discuss several particularly relevant lines of results below.

General downward-closed systems.

For general downward-closed systems, the disjoint-groups example by Babaioff et al. (2007) yields an Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\log n/\log\log n) obstruction already for binary values. In a major breakthrough, Rubinstein (2016) gives O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) guarantees for binary prophet and secretary problems, and a blackbox reduction giving O⁡(log⁡n​log⁡r)=O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log n\log r)=O(\log^{2}n) for general values, where rr is the rank of the feasibility system. Rubinstein and Singla (2026) establish an Ω⁡((log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)2)\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^{2}) prophet lower bound and an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) secretary upper bound, closing the gap up to poly​log⁡log\mathrm{poly}\log\log factors. Our adversarial-order result improves both sides of the former gap, while our prophet-secretary lower bound matches the latter upper bound. In particular, our binary-value upper bound removes an O⁡(log⁡log⁡n)O(\log\log n) factor from the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) binary prophet guarantee of Rubinstein (2016).

Matroid prophet and secretary problems.

Matroids are a natural and well-studied class of feasibility systems. Babaioff et al. (2007) introduce the matroid secretary problem, and also discuss the general downward-closed variant. For general matroids, the sequence of work from (Chakraborty and Lachish, 2012) to (Lachish, 2014) and (Feldman et al., 2015b) improves the secretary guarantee to O⁡(log⁡log⁡r)O(\log\log r), where rr is the rank. The very recent results of (Singla, 2026; Huang, 2026; Abdi et al., 2026) subsequently push the ratio to a constant, and eventually to the optimal ee. On the Bayesian side, Kleinberg and Weinberg (2012) establish the tight factor-two matroid prophet inequality. Online contention resolution provides a related framework for converting fractional solutions into feasible online selections (Feldman et al., 2016). Dütting et al. (2020) give prophet inequalities for a broad range of combinatorial constraints, including matroids, through posted prices. These results exploit structural properties, such as exchange, that arbitrary downward-closed families need not satisfy.

Prophet secretary and related problems.

Esfandiari et al. (2015) introduce the prophet secretary problem, which assumes both uniformly random arrival orders and known independent prior distributions. This is weakly easier than both prophet and secretary. Azar et al. (2017) show that the optimal ratio for this problem is strictly better than 1−1/e1-1/e. Correa et al. (2019b) study blind strategies for the problem. For richer (but structured) feasibility, Ehsani et al. (2024) study prophet secretary for matroids and combinatorial auctions. Jaillet et al. (2013) also study a free-order secretary model subject to matroid feasibility, which changes the order model without supplying known independent value distributions.

Combinatorial objectives and stochastic probing.

Rubinstein and Singla (2017) study prophet inequalities for combinatorial objectives, and the secretary result of Rubinstein and Singla (2026) extends beyond additive objectives to XOS valuations. Combinatorial auctions are another important model for prophet inequalities: Feldman et al. (2015a) study posted-price mechanisms for combinatorial auctions; Dütting et al. (2020) present a unified framework that covers combinatorial auctions; Correa and Cristi (2023) present constant-factor prophet inequalities for subadditive valuations in particular. Stochastic probing separates inspection feasibility from final selection feasibility: Gupta and Nagarajan (2013) formulate this model, Gupta et al. (2017) study submodular and XOS adaptivity gaps, and Li et al. (2025) give bounds for subadditive functions.

Sample-based prophet inequalities.

Azar et al. (2014) systematically study prophet inequalities with limited sample access. Rubinstein et al. (2020) present optimal single-choice prophet inequalities from samples. Caramanis et al. (2022) study greedy-ordered single-sample approaches. Fu et al. (2024) and Feldman et al. (2026) study sample-based prophet inequalities and online contention resolution for matroids.

2 Preliminaries

There are nn items and a known nonempty downward-closed feasibility system ℱ⊆2[n]\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[n]}: every subset of a feasible set is feasible. On observing an item’s nonnegative value, the algorithm must irrevocably accept or reject it, and its accepted items must remain in ℱ\mathcal{F}. For a value vector xx, write

OPT⁡(ℱ;x)=max⁡∑i∈SS∈ℱ⁡xi.\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F};x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}.

This is the (realized) prophet benchmark under xx. We suppress ℱ\mathcal{F} when it is fixed. We allow unrestricted computation.

Standard prophet and free-order prophet.

The values X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} of the nn items are independent random variables with known distributions. The expected prophet benchmark is opt=𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(ℱ,X)]\operatorname{opt}=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F};X)]. In the standard prophet problem the arrival order is fixed adversarially; in the free-order prophet problem the algorithm chooses the order from the priors, before observing the values (our upper bound uses non-adaptive orders). For a fixed order σ\sigma, let algσ\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma} denote the optimal expected online reward. We write alg\operatorname{alg} when the order is clear. A competitive ratio of RR means alg≥opt/R\operatorname{alg}\geq\operatorname{opt}/R on every instance.

Standard secretary and prophet secretary.

In both models the arrival order is a uniformly random permutation. In the standard secretary problem the values xix_{i} are fixed adversarially and not known in advance; here opt=OPT⁡(ℱ,x)\operatorname{opt}=\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F};x) and the guarantee alg≥opt/R\operatorname{alg}\geq\operatorname{opt}/R must hold for each value vector, with expectation over the order and the algorithm’s randomness. In prophet secretary the values have known independent distributions, the permutation is independent of them, and opt=𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(ℱ,X)]\operatorname{opt}=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{F};X)]; the algorithm’s expected reward also averages over the values. Thus opt\operatorname{opt} and alg\operatorname{alg} always denote the prophet benchmark and expected online reward, respectively, with the model-specific expectations just given.

Throughout the paper, we ignore items that are not feasible even as a singleton, as well as those whose expected value is 00. We use (z)+=max⁡{z,0}(z)_{+}=\max\{z,0\} and [a]={1,…,a}[a]=\{1,\ldots,a\} for positive integers aa. Logarithms are natural unless a base is displayed.

3 Lower Bound for the Standard Prophet Problem

Theorem 3.1.

For every sufficiently large nn, there is a downward-closed instance on nn items with independent weighted Bernoulli values and a fixed arrival order, known in advance, on which every online algorithm has competitive ratio Ω⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)\Omega(\log^{2}n/\log\log n).

We keep the notation of the technical overview: layer tt has dtd_{t} coordinates, message mt∈ΣMdtm_{t}\in\Sigma_{M}^{d_{t}}, and codeword ct=ft​(m1,…,mt−1)∈ΣC,tdtc_{t}=f_{t}(m_{1},\ldots,m_{t-1})\in\Sigma_{C,t}^{d_{t}}. Write m<t=(m1,…,mt−1)m_{<t}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{t-1}) and m≤t=(m1,…,mt)m_{\leq t}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{t}). For an integer v≥1v\geq 1, ⌊v⌋pow2\lfloor v\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}} is the largest power of two not exceeding vv. The additional parameter rr is the number of physical items in one group. We first construct an instance for arbitrary integers r,T≥1r,T\geq 1, and then choose both parameters to fit nn items.

3.1 The Construction

Set

dt=2t−1,p=12​r​T,ΣM=[(2​r​T)2​r],d_{t}=2^{t-1},\qquad p=\frac{1}{2rT},\qquad\Sigma_{M}=[(2rT)^{2r}], (2)

where pp is the activation probability of all items. For each layer tt, coordinate i∈[dt]i\in[d_{t}], message symbol b∈ΣMb\in\Sigma_{M}, and codeword symbol s∈ΣC,ts\in\Sigma_{C,t}, create a group G⁡(t,i,b,s)G(t,i,b,s) of rr physical items. All these groups are disjoint. Every item of layer tt has value 1/(r​dt)1/(rd_{t}) with probability pp, and zero otherwise. A message table is a complete sequence of messages (m1,…,mT)(m_{1},\dots,m_{T}) of length TT, where each mt∈ΣMdtm_{t}\in\Sigma_{M}^{d_{t}}. Each message table specifies one maximal feasible set:

⋃t=1T⋃i=1dtG⁡(t,i,(mt)i,(ft​(m<t))i).\bigcup_{t=1}^{T}\ \bigcup_{i=1}^{d_{t}}G\bigl(t,i,(m_{t})_{i},(f_{t}(m_{<t}))_{i}\bigr). (3)

That is, in each layer tt and each coordinate ii, we collect the group G⁡(t,i,(mt)i,(ct)i)G(t,i,(m_{t})_{i},(c_{t})_{i}) where ct=ft​(m<t)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{<t}). The feasibility system consists of all subsets of these sets. Thus at most one group can be used at a coordinate, but all its members may be accepted. The online arrival order is T,T−1,…,1T,T-1,\ldots,1, with any fixed order within each layer.

The code.

One key component in the construction that remains unspecified is the code, captured by ftf_{t}. Intuitively, if two tables first differ in layer τ\tau, we want their codewords to agree on progressively fewer coordinates as t−τt-\tau grows. The lemma below gives the existence of a code that is just strong enough for our purposes, while not requiring an overly large alphabet for codewords. Such overly large alphabets would blow up the number of items and hurt the bound. The proof of the lemma is largely a blackbox combinatorial argument.

Lemma 3.2 (First-divergence-sensitive encoding).

For the coordinate counts in (2), there exist public encoders ftf_{t} with

log⁡|ΣC,t|=O⁡(t+log⁡|ΣM|)\log|\Sigma_{C,t}|=O(t+\log|\Sigma_{M}|)

such that, whenever two tables first differ in layer τ\tau, every t>τt>\tau satisfies

|ct∩ct′|dt≤14​⌊t−τ⌋pow2 2.\frac{|c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}|}{d_{t}}\leq\frac{1}{4\lfloor t-\tau\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}^{\,2}}. (4)

Here |ct∩ct′||c_{t}\cap c_{t}^{\prime}| is the number of agreeing coordinates, as in the overview. These encoders lead to at most n=exp⁡(O⁡(T+r​log⁡(2​r​T)))n=\exp(O(T+r\log(2rT))) items per the construction.

Proof.

We first give the elementary coding fact used in the construction. Suppose there are NN possible inputs, the desired word length is mm, and 0<δ≤10<\delta\leq 1. Put

k=⌈δ​m⌉,Q=⌈2​eδ​N1/k⌉.k=\lceil\delta m\rceil,\qquad Q=\left\lceil\frac{2e}{\delta}N^{1/k}\right\rceil.

A uniformly random word in [Q]m[Q]^{m} agrees with a fixed word on a prescribed set of kk coordinates with probability Q−kQ^{-k}. Its probability of agreeing on at least kk coordinates is therefore at most

(mk)​Q−k≤(eδ​Q)k≤2−kN.\binom{m}{k}Q^{-k}\leq\left(\frac{e}{\delta Q}\right)^{k}\leq\frac{2^{-k}}{N}.

Choose the words one at a time. Fewer than NN previously chosen words forbid strictly less than the whole space of possible next words, so all NN inputs can be assigned words with at most k−1<δ​mk-1<\delta m agreements per pair. The alphabet satisfies

log⁡Q=O⁡(log⁡(2/δ)+log⁡Nδ​m).\log Q=O\left(\log(2/\delta)+\frac{\log N}{\delta m}\right). (5)

This is an existence argument; the code is fixed before the item values are drawn.

For each h∈{1,2,4,…}h\in\{1,2,4,\ldots\} with h<th<t, apply this fact to all prefixes m≤t−hm_{\leq t-h}, using length dtd_{t} and δ=1/(4​h2)\delta=1/(4h^{2}). At coordinate ii, let (ft​(m<t))i(f_{t}(m_{<t}))_{i} be the tuple of the component symbols at that coordinate. For t=1t=1 the tuple is empty and the code alphabet has one symbol. If the first divergence is τ<t\tau<t, take h=⌊t−τ⌋pow2h=\lfloor t-\tau\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}. Since t−h≥τt-h\geq\tau, the protected prefixes differ. Their component codewords agree on fewer than dt/(4​h2)d_{t}/(4h^{2}) coordinates. Full tuples can agree only at these coordinates, which proves (4).

The number of message symbols in the prefix through t−ht-h is

∑s=1t−hds=2t−h−1<2​dt​ 2−h.\sum_{s=1}^{t-h}d_{s}=2^{t-h}-1<2d_{t}\,2^{-h}.

Consequently (5) bounds the logarithm of the component alphabet by O⁡(log⁡(2​h)+h2​2−h​log⁡|ΣM|)O(\log(2h)+h^{2}2^{-h}\log|\Sigma_{M}|). Taking products of the alphabets, and hence sums of their logarithms, gives

Remark.

No code separates two choices of the current message immediately: when the first divergence is in layer τ\tau, its inherited codewords in the same layer coincide. We use the trivial overlap bound one in that layer. In later layers the bounds in (4) sum to O⁡(1)O(1). This, rather than uniformly tiny overlap at every gap, is the property used below.

3.2 The Prophet Benchmark

Lemma 3.3.

(1−e−1)​T≤opt≤T.(1-e^{-1})T\leq\operatorname{opt}\leq T.

Consider a partial prophet that sees all the realized values in each layer upon entering that layer. 1−(1−pr)|ΣM|≥1−e−|ΣM|​pr=1−e−p−r≥1−e−1.1-(1-p^{r})^{|\Sigma_{M}|}\geq 1-e^{-|\Sigma_{M}|p^{r}}=1-e^{-p^{-r}}\geq 1-e^{-1}.
