3.3 The Algorithm’s Performance

Intuition.

The algorithm is forced to visit layers in the order of T,…,1T,\dots,1. In each layer, the first acceptance at a coordinate can be unusually valuable: the algorithm has inspected its value before choosing its group. After that acceptance, unseen members of the chosen group have activation probability pp, and the expected contribution is discounted by that probability. We bound these two contributions separately. The first contributions are counted ex post using two viable tables (this realizes the first-divergence intuition discussed in the technical overview); the remaining contributions are bounded in expectation at the time the group is fixed (similar to the lower bound by Babaioff et al. (2007)).

Lemma 3.4.

Every online algorithm for the construction above, in the order T,T−1,…,1T,T-1,\ldots,1, has expected reward at most 2/r2/r.

Proof.

Fix an optimal online algorithm and bound alg\operatorname{alg}. Consider a realized execution of the algorithm. At a certain time in the execution, a message table is viable if its maximal feasible set contains every item accepted so far. Feasibility ensures that some table is always viable. We call a layer tt determined if, at entry to layer tt, all viable tables agree on m≤tm_{\leq t}, and ambiguous otherwise. Further acceptances only remove viable tables. Moreover, moving from layer tt to layer t−1t-1 shortens the prefix on which agreement is required. Thus determined layers form a suffix of the visited layers and ambiguous layers form a prefix.

Let NtN_{t} be the number of “touched” coordinates of layer tt, i.e., coordinates at which the algorithm accepts at least one item. We first prove

alg≤Tp+1r𝔼[∑t:ambiguous entryNtdt].\operatorname{alg}\leq Tp+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t:\text{ambiguous entry}\end{subarray}}\frac{N_{t}}{d_{t}}\right]. (6)

At a determined entry to layer tt, the common prefix fixes one group of items at every coordinate of layer tt. Realized values in this layer are still uncertain. Conditional on the entry history, the sum of all values in these r​dtrd_{t} items has expectation pp, which is an upper bound on the algorithm’s reward in that layer.

At an ambiguous entry to layer tt, charge the first acceptance at each touched coordinate the activated value of an item, 1/(r​dt)1/(rd_{t}). Immediately after that acceptance, the group at the coordinate is fixed. There are NtN_{t} touched coordinates, so the first acceptances contribute Nt/(r​dt)N_{t}/(rd_{t}). As for the subsequent acceptances in each group, conditional on the history right after the first acceptance, at most r−1r-1 members of this group remain unseen; each still has expected value p/(r​dt)p/(rd_{t}). Members seen and rejected earlier are unavailable. All later acceptances at this coordinate therefore have conditional expected total value at most p/dtp/d_{t}. Summing over the dtd_{t} coordinates gives at most pp, which bounds the total value of the subsequent acceptances in the layer. Finally, summing over layers tt gives (6).

It remains to bound the sum in (6) on every realized play (i.e., we will bound the sum inside the expectation directly). If no entry is ambiguous, it is zero. Otherwise let ss be the last ambiguous layer in arrival order as perceived by the algorithm. At its entry, choose any two viable tables that differ in their prefixes through ss, and let τ≤s\tau\leq s be the layer of their first divergence.99 9 Note that τ\tau may not be ss, since acceptances made in layer ss may eliminate viable tables, and all we know is that after such eliminations, all viable tables agree up to layer s−1s-1. Every layer t>st>s has already finished. At every one of its NtN_{t} touched coordinates, both tables contain an accepted item. Since groups are disjoint, both tables use the same group there; in particular, their codeword symbols agree. Lemma 3.2 gives

Ntdt≤14​⌊t−τ⌋pow2 2≤14​⌊t−s⌋pow2 2(t>s).\frac{N_{t}}{d_{t}}\leq\frac{1}{4\lfloor t-\tau\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}^{\,2}}\leq\frac{1}{4\lfloor t-s\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}^{\,2}}\qquad(t>s).

The second inequality uses τ≤s\tau\leq s. Again, the pair of witness tables need not remain viable through layer ss as more acceptances are made, so we bound Ns/dsN_{s}/d_{s} simply by one. No layer t<st<s has an ambiguous entry. Consequently,

∑t:ambiguous entryNtdt≤1+∑v=1∞14​⌊v⌋pow2 2=1+∑h=1,2,4,…h4​h2=32.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t:\text{ambiguous entry}\end{subarray}}\frac{N_{t}}{d_{t}}\leq 1+\sum_{v=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{4\lfloor v\rfloor_{\mathrm{pow2}}^{\,2}}=1+\sum_{h=1,2,4,\ldots}\frac{h}{4h^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}.

The same pair of tables bounds all completed layers. Its retrospective choice is legitimate because the argument is ex post. Substitution into (6), with T​p=1/(2​r)Tp=1/(2r), proves the lemma. ∎

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

The preceding two lemmas give ratio at least (1−e−1)​r​T/2(1-e^{-1})rT/2. For a sufficiently small absolute constant c>0c>0, choose

r=⌊c​log⁡nlog⁡log⁡n⌋,T=⌊c​log⁡n⌋.r=\left\lfloor c\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right\rfloor,\qquad T=\lfloor c\log n\rfloor.

Both are positive for sufficiently large nn. Since log⁡(2​r​T)=O⁡(log⁡log⁡n)\log(2rT)=O(\log\log n), the item bound in Lemma 3.2 is at most nn after decreasing cc if necessary. The resulting ratio is Ω⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)\Omega(\log^{2}n/\log\log n), as claimed. ∎

4 Lower Bound for the Prophet Secretary Problem

Theorem 4.1.

For every sufficiently large nn, there is a downward-closed instance on nn independent weighted Bernoulli items on which every prophet-secretary algorithm has competitive ratio Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n), even when the entire permutation is announced before play. The same bound applies to the standard secretary problem by extension.

We continue to use dtd_{t} for the coordinate count, mtm_{t} for the message, and ct=ft​(m<t)c_{t}=f_{t}(m_{<t}) for the codeword in layer tt. There is now one item per pair of symbols at a coordinate, not a group. As discussed momentarily, the code in this construction encodes only the specified prefixes of earlier message symbols, which is different from the adversarial-order construction.

4.1 The Construction

Fix an integer T≥2T\geq 2 and put

dt=T​2t−1,ΣM={0,1}T,ΣC=[24​T].d_{t}=T2^{t-1},\qquad\Sigma_{M}=\{0,1\}^{T},\qquad\Sigma_{C}=[2^{4T}]. (7)

In particular, note that here we use the same codeword alphabet for all layers. The subscript tt is therefore omitted. For each t∈[T]t\in[T], i∈[dt]i\in[d_{t}], a∈ΣMa\in\Sigma_{M}, and b∈ΣCb\in\Sigma_{C}, create one item (t,i,a,b)(t,i,a,b). Its value realizes to 1/dt1/d_{t} with probability 2−T2^{-T}, and zero otherwise, independently of every other item. Every message table (m1,…,mT)(m_{1},\ldots,m_{T}) specifies one maximal feasible set:

{(t,i,(mt)i,(ft(m<t))i):t∈[T],i∈[dt]}.\{(t,i,(m_{t})_{i},(f_{t}(m_{<t}))_{i}):t\in[T],\ i\in[d_{t}]\}.

Take all subsets of these sets are also feasible. The number of items is

25​T​∑t=1Tdt=T⁡(2T−1)​25​T≤T​26​T.2^{5T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}=T(2^{T}-1)2^{5T}\leq T2^{6T}. (8)

Each feasible set uses at most one item at a coordinate, so its value is at most one per layer and at most TT in total.

The code that encodes nested prefixes.

In layer tt, the encoder reads the first t−τt-\tau bits of every symbol of mτm_{\tau}, for every layer τ<t\tau<t. Thus the layer-two codeword depends on one bit of every layer-one message symbol. The layer-three codeword depends on two bits of each layer-one message symbol and one bit of each layer-two message symbol, etc.

The encoded prefixes are nested, so the codeword in a later layer encodes all the bits encoded by an earlier-layer codeword, as well as additional bits. The doubling of dtd_{t} ensures that the number of encoded bits is still proportional to the current codeword length. Again, in the execution of an online algorithm, we call a message table viable if it is consistent with the items accepted so far. The following lemma captures the guarantee we need from the code.

Lemma 4.2 (Recovery of nested message prefixes).

There are encoders with the alphabets in (7) such that ctc_{t} depends exactly on the protected bits as described, and any

kt=dt/T=2t−1k_{t}=d_{t}/T=2^{t-1}

codeword symbols, together with their coordinate indices, determine those bits uniquely. In particular, once a feasible algorithm has accepted kuk_{u} items in layer uu, all viable message tables have the same codeword ctc_{t} for every t≤ut\leq u, and the same first u−tu-t bits of each symbol of mtm_{t}. At a coordinate in layer t≤ut\leq u, at most 2T−u+t2^{T-u+t} items can remain compatible with this recovered information.

Proof.

Fix a public order in which to concatenate the encoded bits. The total number of such bits in layer tt (i.e., those in the messages of earlier layers τ\tau that are encoded by ct=ftc_{t}=f_{t}) is

∑τ<t(t−τ)​dτ=dt​∑h=1t−1h​2−h<2​dt.\sum_{\tau<t}(t-\tau)d_{\tau}=d_{t}\sum_{h=1}^{t-1}h2^{-h}<2d_{t}.

The last strict inequality follows from ∑h≥1h​2−h=2\sum_{h\geq 1}h2^{-h}=2. There are fewer than 22​dt2^{2d_{t}} possible strings of such encoded bits. Assign each such string a codeword in ΣCdt\Sigma_{C}^{d_{t}} greedily to minimize overlap with already chosen codewords. For a fixed previous codeword, a uniformly random codeword agrees with it at any prescribed ktk_{t} positions with probability (24​T)−kt(2^{4T})^{-k_{t}}. The fraction of candidates agreeing in at least ktk_{t} positions is at most

(dtkt)​2−4​T​kt≤2dt−4​dt=2−3​dt.\binom{d_{t}}{k_{t}}2^{-4Tk_{t}}\leq 2^{d_{t}-4d_{t}}=2^{-3d_{t}}.

Even the union of the forbidden candidates from all fewer than 22​dt2^{2d_{t}} previous assignments has fraction below one. So a next codeword exists. Therefore different strings of encoded bits receive codewords agreeing in fewer than ktk_{t} coordinates. In layer one, the encoded string is empty and its single codeword can be chosen arbitrarily. Define ftf_{t} by first reading the encoded bits and then applying this fixed assignment.

Feasibility forces any kuk_{u} accepted layer-uu items into distinct coordinates. Their codeword symbols identify the encoded string uniquely by the property of the code constructed and proved above. For t<ut<u, the encoded string contains the first u−tu-t bits of each layer-tt message symbol. It also contains every bit needed to compute ctc_{t}, because u−τ≥t−τu-\tau\geq t-\tau for every τ<t\tau<t. The word cuc_{u} itself is uniquely recovered as well. Consequently a coordinate in layer t≤ut\leq u has a fixed codeword symbol and a fixed message prefix of length u−tu-t. There are exactly 2T−u+t2^{T-u+t} possible completions of that prefix. At t=ut=u the prefix is empty; the codeword symbol is fixed but all 2T2^{T} message symbols remain available. Every viable table obeys these restrictions, which proves the last assertion. ∎

Remark (Reed-Solomon also suffices).

The greedy construction is provided to be self-contained. One can instead use the Reed-Solomon code (Reed and Solomon, 1960) directly: pad the protected string to 2​dt2d_{t} bits, regard it as kt=dt/Tk_{t}=d_{t}/T coefficients over 𝔽22​T\mathbb{F}_{2^{2T}}, and evaluate the resulting polynomial of degree at most kt−1k_{t}-1 at dtd_{t} distinct field points. Such points exist because dt≤T​2T−1≤22​Td_{t}\leq T2^{T-1}\leq 2^{2T}. Any ktk_{t} evaluations determine the polynomial: the difference of two such polynomials has degree below ktk_{t} and cannot have ktk_{t} distinct roots unless it is zero. This gives the same recovery property with an alphabet that embeds in ΣC\Sigma_{C}.

4.2 The Prophet Benchmark

Lemma 4.3.

The construction above satisfies

(1−e−1)​T≤opt≤T.(1-e^{-1})T\leq\operatorname{opt}\leq T.

Moreover, an online algorithm in the fixed layer order 1,…,T1,\ldots,T achieves expected reward at least (1−e−1)​T(1-e^{-1})T.

Proof.

The upper bound is immediate from at most one item per coordinate and value 1/dt1/d_{t} per item. For the lower bound, it suffices to describe the stated online algorithm. Before processing layer tt, it has completed messages m1,…,mt−1m_{1},\ldots,m_{t-1}, so it can compute ctc_{t}. At each coordinate, it accepts the first active item whose codeword symbol agrees with ctc_{t} and ignores all other items at that coordinate. At the end of the layer, fill any message coordinates at which no item was accepted with arbitrary symbols. Every such completion is allowed and is consistent with all previous acceptances. Thus the algorithm remains feasible.

Conditional on the earlier layers, a coordinate offers 2T2^{T} independent items with the codeword symbol fixed. Each is active with probability 2−T2^{-T}, so the probability of at least one success is

1−(1−2−T)2T≥1−e−1.1-(1-2^{-T})^{2^{T}}\geq 1-e^{-1}.

A successful coordinate contributes 1/dt1/d_{t}. Summing first over coordinates and then over layers proves the expected-reward guarantee. The prophet can choose at least the same feasible set on every realization. ∎

4.3 Constrained and Unconstrained Acceptances

In order to bound the performance of online algorithms, we need to define a few auxiliary concepts. Immediately before each item’s value is revealed, define the cutoff layer by

u=max({t:at least kt items have already been accepted in layer t}∪{0}),kt=dt/T.u=\max\bigl(\{t:\text{at least }k_{t}\text{ items have already been accepted in layer }t\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),\qquad k_{t}=d_{t}/T.

The cutoff never decreases throughout the algorithm’s execution. An acceptance in layer t>ut>u is unconstrained, and one in layer t≤ut\leq u is constrained (tt is the layer containing the item being accepted, and uu is the cutoff layer right before that acceptance). Note that these names refer only to the restrictions certified by the cutoff; other accepted items can impose further feasibility restrictions. The state used for the above classification is always the one before the current value is observed. In particular, an acceptance that raises uu is unconstrained.

Below we first bound the total contribution of unconstrained acceptances, which is the easier part of the argument.

Lemma 4.4.

The total realized reward of unconstrained acceptances is at most one.

Proof.

Once the ktk_{t}-th item is accepted in layer tt, the cutoff is at least tt forever. Hence layer tt can contribute at most ktk_{t} unconstrained acceptances, including the acceptance that first reaches the threshold. Every item in the layer is worth at most 1/dt1/d_{t}, so their total value is at most

∑t=1Tktdt=1.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{k_{t}}{d_{t}}=1.

This argument is ex post and makes no restriction on how observed values influence the acceptance decisions. ∎

It remains to bound the expected reward of constrained acceptances. At a positive cutoff uu, Lemma 4.2 gives a uniquely determined codeword cuc_{u} and restricts the eligible identities in all layers t≤ut\leq u. For a fixed codeword cuc_{u}, the total mean of all compatible items in layer tt is at most 2t−u2^{t-u}, so the sum over these layers is less than two. This is a mean calculation that gives an intuitive bound, not yet a formal one that works for the actual algorithm. The next reduction addresses that distinction.

4.4 The Harvesting Game

Consider the following relaxed setting that grants more power to the algorithm (or the harvester in this setting). It focuses solely on constrained acceptances; unconstrained acceptances have already been bounded earlier. Generate the permutation of items by assigning each item independently to a uniform bin in [T][T], ordering each bin uniformly at random, and concatenating the bins. The resulting permutation is uniform. Bin sizes are random. Announce the entire permutation and the bin assignments before the first arrival; write 𝒟\mathcal{D} for this announcement. Note that all this is independent of all item values.

A harvester keeps a cutoff u∈{0,…,T}u\in\{0,\ldots,T\} and, when u>0u>0, a declaration cuc_{u} that is a possible codeword in layer uu. The declaration determines codeword symbols and message prefixes in layers t≤ut\leq u as in Lemma 4.2. All items in these layers whose message and codeword symbols are consistent with cuc_{u} are considered compatible. Initially u=0u=0, cuc_{u} is empty, and there are no compatible items. The rules at the beginning of a bin are as follows. First the harvester collects the entire value of every compatible item in that bin under its current declaration, inherited from the previous bin. It may then make any number of strict cutoff increases, where it replaces uu with an integer between u+1u+1 and TT. At each increase, it declares an arbitrary possible codeword cuc_{u} for the new layer uu and collects every item of the current bin compatible with the newly declared uu and cuc_{u}. Successive declarations need not be consistent. We ignore feasibility restrictions (which gives the harvester more power), but an item contributes only once, at its first harvest. Crucially, the declaration is chosen before the newly harvested values are revealed (otherwise the harvester would be too powerful). The harvester observes no other values. It may use earlier harvests to decide on further increases and declarations, and it carries its last declaration into the next bin. There are at most TT cutoff increases, in addition to one carried harvest per bin. Several increases in the same bin are permitted and can collect different items.

The following lemma connects the harvesting game to constrained acceptances made by an actual online algorithm.

Lemma 4.5 (Reduction to harvesting).

Conditional on any announcement 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the expected reward of the constrained acceptances of any online algorithm (that can even depend on 𝒟\mathcal{D}) is at most the optimal conditional expected reward in the harvesting game.

Proof.

Fix 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Given an online algorithm, we construct a strategy in the harvesting game that produces at least as much conditional expected reward as the algorithm’s constrained acceptances. For each item ii, let JiJ_{i} be the indicator that, immediately before its value is revealed, its layer satisfies t≤ut\leq u and its identity is compatible with the codeword cuc_{u} already determined by previous acceptances. This is an eligibility indicator, not an acceptance indicator. Every constrained acceptance has Ji=1J_{i}=1, by Lemma 4.2, and nonnegative values therefore give the ex post upper bound

constrained reward≤∑iJi​Xi.\text{constrained reward}\leq\sum_{i}J_{i}X_{i}.

Given 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the history immediately before this arrival, JiJ_{i} is known and XiX_{i} retains its prior mean. Independence gives

𝔼⁡[Ji​Xi∣𝒟]=𝔼⁡[Ji∣𝒟]​𝔼​[Xi].\mathbb{E}[J_{i}X_{i}\mid\mathcal{D}]=\mathbb{E}[J_{i}\mid\mathcal{D}]\,\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]. (9)

This holds even though the subsequent acceptance decision can depend on XiX_{i}. If that decision raises the cutoff, its own reward is already unconstrained; the new codeword is used only for subsequent eligibility.

Fix a realized execution of the original algorithm. In each bin, record its carried cutoff upon entry and every subsequent strict increase, with the corresponding uniquely determined codewords. Move that entire list of declarations to the opening of the bin and keep their order. This is a structurally legal schedule (not to be confused with an actual strategy; see discussion below): cutoffs increase strictly when changed, and arbitrary declarations are allowed. While the cutoff is fixed, the recovered codeword cannot change, because further acceptances only remove viable tables. The problem is that the schedule depends on the realized values, and therefore cannot be implemented in the stated form by the harvester who does not see the values upon entering a bin. We will turn the schedule into an actual strategy later through simulation of the algorithm on phantom values.

Back to the above schedule: every item with Ji=1J_{i}=1 lies in a harvest of this schedule, because its pre-arrival declaration occurs in the list for its own bin. Therefore

∑iJi​𝔼​[Xi]≤∑i​ is harvested𝔼⁡[Xi].\sum_{i}J_{i}\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\leq\sum_{i\text{ is harvested}}\mathbb{E}[X_{i}].

Here, the right side sums over the union of the recorded harvests, counting each item only once.

To implement an actual, executable strategy, before any arrival, draw independent phantom values from all the priors and independent copies of the original algorithm’s random coins. Simulate that algorithm on these virtual values with the same announcement 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and record the resulting schedule as above. Execute this schedule on the actual values, without using the actual harvest observations to change its declarations. This is legal: all declarations are chosen using only 𝒟\mathcal{D} and private randomness, independently of the actual values. Conditional on the simulated schedule, its expected harvest is exactly the sum of the prior means in its harvested union.

The simulated execution has the same conditional distribution as the original execution. Consequently the expected sum of means in its recorded union is at least 𝔼⁡[∑iJi​𝔼​[Xi]∣𝒟]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i}J_{i}\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\mid\mathcal{D}], by the ex post inequality above. Applying (9) and summing over items gives

𝔼⁡[harvesting reward∣𝒟]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\text{harvesting reward}\mid\mathcal{D}] ≥𝔼⁡[∑iJi​𝔼​[Xi]|𝒟]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}J_{i}\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\,\middle|\,\mathcal{D}\right]
=𝔼⁡[∑iJi​Xi|𝒟]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}J_{i}X_{i}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{D}\right]
≥𝔼⁡[constrained reward∣𝒟].\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[\text{constrained reward}\mid\mathcal{D}].

The JiJ_{i} and XiX_{i} in the last two expressions refer to the original online execution; equality in distribution justifies the comparison with the phantom record. This proves the reduction lemma. ∎

4.5 Bounding the Contribution of Constrained Acceptances

With the reduction to the harvesting game established, we are ready to bound the contribution of constrained acceptances. For a possible declaration cuc_{u}, let its menu M⁡(cu)M(c_{u}) be all items in layers t≤ut\leq u compatible with the codeword symbols and message prefixes recovered from cuc_{u}. Put M⁡(c0)=∅M(c_{0})=\varnothing. A harvest in bin BjB_{j} collects M⁡(cu)∩BjM(c_{u})\cap B_{j}.

As in the overview, a piece Pt,i,s,pP_{t,i,s,p} fixes a layer tt, a coordinate ii, a codeword symbol s∈ΣCs\in\Sigma_{C}, and a binary prefix pp of length at most TT. It consists of all items (t,i,a,s)(t,i,a,s) with aa extending pp; hence |Pt,i,s,p|=2T−|p||P_{t,i,s,p}|=2^{T-|p|}, where |p||p| is the length of pp as a binary string. Every menu is a disjoint union of one piece per coordinate of each layer t≤ut\leq u. In that layer the prescribed prefix has length u−tu-t. Its piece therefore has size 2T−u+t2^{T-u+t}, and each of its items has mean 1/(2T​dt)1/(2^{T}d_{t}).

Intuition: all menus are evenly distributed across bins.

A fixed menu has total mean less than two. A uniform bin should receive about a 1/T1/T fraction of this mean. The algorithm knows the bin assignment, so this estimate must hold simultaneously for all possible declarations of codewords. There are too many complete declarations for a direct union bound. Instead, there are fewer than twice as many pieces as items. Concentrating each piece suffices for every menu.

Lemma 4.6 (Uniform bin bounds for pieces and menus).

With probability at least

1−2​T2​exp⁡(−(10−6​log⁡2)​T)1-2T^{2}\exp\bigl(-(10-6\log 2)T\bigr)

over the independent bin assignments, every piece Pt,i,s,pP_{t,i,s,p} and bin BjB_{j} satisfy

|Pt,i,s,p∩Bj|≤e−1T​|Pt,i,s,p|+10​T.|P_{t,i,s,p}\cap B_{j}|\leq\frac{e-1}{T}|P_{t,i,s,p}|+10T. (10)

On the same event, for every possible declaration cuc_{u} and every bin,

∑a∈M⁡(cu)∩Bj𝔼⁡[Xa]≤2​(e−1)T+10​T22T.\sum_{a\in M(c_{u})\cap B_{j}}\mathbb{E}[X_{a}]\leq\frac{2(e-1)}{T}+\frac{10T^{2}}{2^{T}}. (11)

The second bound concerns the sum of the prior means, conditional on the announced (indices of) items and bins.

Proof.

Fix a piece PP and bin BjB_{j}. The independent bin assignments make |P∩Bj||P\cap B_{j}| binomial with parameters |P||P| and 1/T1/T. Therefore

𝔼⁡[e|P∩Bj|]=(1+(e−1)/T)|P|≤exp⁡((e−1)​|P|/T).\mathbb{E}[e^{|P\cap B_{j}|}]=\bigl(1+(e-1)/T\bigr)^{|P|}\leq\exp\bigl((e-1)|P|/T\bigr).

Markov’s inequality gives

Pr[|P∩Bj|>(e−1)|P|/T+10T]≤e−10​T.\Pr\bigl[|P\cap B_{j}|>(e-1)|P|/T+10T\bigr]\leq e^{-10T}.

For each coordinate and codeword symbol there are 2T+1−12^{T+1}-1 prefixes, including the empty prefix and all full strings. Hence the number of pieces is less than twice the number of physical items in (8), and the number of piece–bin pairs is at most 2​T2​26​T2T^{2}2^{6T}. The union bound proves (10) simultaneously, with the stated failure probability. This event depends only on the bin assignments.

Fix any assignment on this event, any declaration, and any bin. Summing (10) over the dtd_{t} pieces of each layer in the menu, and weighting each item by its mean, yields

∑a∈M⁡(cu)∩Bj𝔼⁡[Xa]\displaystyle\sum_{a\in M(c_{u})\cap B_{j}}\mathbb{E}[X_{a}] ≤∑t=1udt2T​dt​(e−1T​2T−u+t+10​T)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{u}\frac{d_{t}}{2^{T}d_{t}}\left(\frac{e-1}{T}2^{T-u+t}+10T\right)
≤e−1T​∑t=1u2t−u+10​u​T2T≤2​(e−1)T+10​T22T.\displaystyle\leq\frac{e-1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{u}2^{t-u}+\frac{10uT}{2^{T}}\leq\frac{2(e-1)}{T}+\frac{10T^{2}}{2^{T}}.

For u=0u=0 the menu is empty. This proves the uniform menu bound. ∎

Remark.

The additive term in (10) cannot in general be removed for each piece: a singleton has occupancy one in its assigned bin, however small its mean occupancy 1/T1/T was. Its aggregated mean-value cost is negligible because each item’s activation probability includes 2−T2^{-T}.

Now we can bound the contribution of constrained acceptances.

Lemma 4.7.

Every online algorithm, even given 𝒟\mathcal{D}, has expected reward from constrained acceptances at most

4​(e−1)+20​T32T+2​T3​exp⁡(−(10−6​log⁡2)​T)=4​(e−1)+o⁡(1).4(e-1)+\frac{20T^{3}}{2^{T}}+2T^{3}\exp\bigl(-(10-6\log 2)T\bigr)=4(e-1)+o(1).
Proof.

Fix an announcement 𝒟\mathcal{D} satisfying Lemma 4.6. Any execution of any harvesting strategy opens at most TT carried menus and TT new menus from strict cutoff increases. Immediately before each harvest, condition on the harvester’s observations and random choices so far. Every newly harvested item is still unobserved and contributes its mean. Thus the conditional expected gain from this harvest is at most the sum of the means in the current bin–menu intersection. Summing these conditional bounds over at most 2​T2T harvests bounds the strategy’s expected reward. By (11), this is at most

2​T​(2​(e−1)T+10​T22T)=4​(e−1)+20​T32T.2T\left(\frac{2(e-1)}{T}+\frac{10T^{2}}{2^{T}}\right)=4(e-1)+\frac{20T^{3}}{2^{T}}.

The bound applies to all strategies selected using the announcement. Lemma 4.5 therefore gives the same upper bound for the conditional expected constrained reward of the original algorithm.

On an exceptional announcement (where concentration fails), the original algorithm still returns a feasible set of realized value at most TT. Multiplying this bound by the failure probability in Lemma 4.6 and averaging proves the claim. ∎

This finally gives us all the pieces needed to prove the main theorem in this section.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Lemmas 4.4 and 4.7 bound the online value by 1+4​(e−1)+o​(1)1+4(e-1)+o(1), while Lemma 4.3 gives opt≥(1−e−1)​T\operatorname{opt}\geq(1-e^{-1})T. For a small enough absolute constant c>0c>0, choose T=⌊c​log⁡n⌋T=\lfloor c\log n\rfloor. Equation (8) then gives at most nn genuine items. This gives the desired lower bound of Ω⁡(T)=Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(T)=\Omega(\log n) for the prophet secretary problem. The same bound holds for the standard secretary problem. ∎

5 Upper Bound for the Standard Prophet Problem

Theorem 5.1.

For independent nonnegative integrable values and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility on nn items, the standard prophet problem admits competitive ratio O⁡(log2⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)O(\log^{2}n/\log\log n).

For a residual downward-closed system 𝒮\mathcal{S} on the unseen items, let OPT⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S}) denote its realized prophet benchmark and alg⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}) the optimal expected additional online reward in the inherited order. Neither includes rewards already obtained. For a next item ii, use the deletion and contraction notation from the overview:

𝒮∖i={S∈𝒮:i∉S},𝒮/i={S∖{i}:S∈𝒮,i∈S}.\mathcal{S}\setminus i=\{S\in\mathcal{S}:i\notin S\},\qquad\mathcal{S}/i=\{S\setminus\{i\}:S\in\mathcal{S},\ i\in S\}.

Downward closure makes contraction a subset of deletion. These definitions are used in the continuation arguments in this section and the next one.

The core of the proof is an improved bound for the case with binary values. This immediately extends to the general problem through a blackbox reduction by Rubinstein (2016). We first present the bound for binary values and show how it implies the main theorem of the section.

Lemma 5.2 (Binary prophet bound).

If all item values lie in {0,1}\{0,1\}, then in every residual instance defined by 𝒮\mathcal{S} with mm items, and for every a≥2a\geq 2,

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]≤exp⁡(2​(a+log⁡(m+1))​alg⁡(𝒮)).\mathbb{E}\bigl[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}\bigr]\leq\exp\bigl(2(a+\log(m+1))\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S})\bigr). (12)

As a result, the binary standard prophet problem has competitive ratio O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n). Both statements also hold when the arrival-order adversary may choose the next unseen identity using only previously revealed values and decisions, and alg\operatorname{alg} is the optimal guaranteed reward against that adversary.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

The value-band extension of Rubinstein (2016, proof of Corollary 1) turns a binary prophet guarantee into a general-value guarantee at an additional factor O⁡(log⁡(ρ+1))O(\log(\rho+1)), where ρ\rho is the largest cardinality of a feasible set. Apply this black-box extension with the binary guarantee in Lemma 5.2. Since ρ≤n\rho\leq n, the resulting ratio is

O⁡(log⁡nlog⁡log⁡n​log⁡(ρ+1))=O⁡(log2⁡nlog⁡log⁡n).∎O\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\log(\rho+1)\right)=O\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{\log\log n}\right).\qed

Now we come back to the binary case. The proof analyzes the optimal online algorithm, which is implicit but satisfies certain recurrences that follow from optimality. The ideas are discussed below.

Intuition for the binary induction.

From any residual problem onward, fixing the next item to arrive, there are two possible continuations: either we accept the item, which gives immediate reward but limits future options, or we reject the item and keep more freedom. The two continuations apply to both the prophet and the algorithm. The prophet can compare both feasible continuations after seeing the future, whereas the algorithm compares only their expectations. Examining the moment generating function of the prophet benchmark lets us charge the prophet’s extra power to the online gain up to a factor of O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n). If accepting an active item gives the algorithm a large improvement, that improvement pays for the extra power directly. Otherwise, acceptance has already lost at least half a unit of expected continuation value. The exponential penalty for that loss pays for the extra power instead.

Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Fix a≥2a\geq 2 and put bm=2​(a+log⁡(m+1))b_{m}=2(a+\log(m+1)). We prove (12) by induction on mm. With no remaining items, both OPT\operatorname{OPT} and alg\operatorname{alg} are zero and the two sides equal one. Let ii be the next item. Abbreviate the continuation values by alg0=alg⁡(𝒮∖i)\operatorname{alg}_{0}=\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}\setminus i) and alg1=alg⁡(𝒮/i)\operatorname{alg}_{1}=\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}/i), and the corresponding offline values by OPT0,OPT1\operatorname{OPT}_{0},\operatorname{OPT}_{1} on the same future realization. If ii is a loop (i.e., it is infeasible even as a singleton), then the contraction continuation does not exist, and we use the induction hypothesis for deletion and bm≥bm−1b_{m}\geq b_{m-1}. Now assume ii is feasible. Downward closure gives alg0≥alg1\operatorname{alg}_{0}\geq\operatorname{alg}_{1} and OPT0≥OPT1\operatorname{OPT}_{0}\geq\operatorname{OPT}_{1}. Independence leaves the remaining priors unchanged after observing XiX_{i}. Writing pi=Pr⁡(Xi=1)p_{i}=\Pr(X_{i}=1) and Δ=(1+alg1−alg0)+∈[0,1]\Delta=(1+\operatorname{alg}_{1}-\operatorname{alg}_{0})_{+}\in[0,1], the online recurrence is

alg=alg0+pi​Δ.\operatorname{alg}=\operatorname{alg}_{0}+p_{i}\Delta. (13)

An inactive item may be rejected without loss.

The two offline continuation values are integers. If Xi=1X_{i}=1, including ii improves the deletion optimum precisely when OPT1=OPT0\operatorname{OPT}_{1}=\operatorname{OPT}_{0}, and then by one. If Xi=0X_{i}=0, the optimum equals OPT0\operatorname{OPT}_{0}. Therefore

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}] =𝔼[aOPT0]+pi(a−1)𝔼[aOPT1𝟏{OPT1=OPT0}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{0}}]+p_{i}(a-1)\mathbb{E}\bigl[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}}\mathbf{1}_{\{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}=\operatorname{OPT}_{0}\}}\bigr]
≤𝔼⁡[aOPT0]+pi​(a−1)​𝔼​[aOPT1].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{0}}]+p_{i}(a-1)\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}}]. (14)

We compare the inductive bounds for these two terms with ebm​alge^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}}.

Case 1: Δ>1/2\Delta>1/2. In this case pi≤2​pi​Δp_{i}\leq 2p_{i}\Delta. Both child moments are at most ebm​alg0e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}_{0}}, since bm−1≤bmb_{m-1}\leq b_{m} and alg1≤alg0\operatorname{alg}_{1}\leq\operatorname{alg}_{0}. Consequently

𝔼⁡[aOPT⁡(𝒮)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal{S})}] ≤ebm​alg0​(1+2​(a−1)​pi​Δ)\displaystyle\leq e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}_{0}}\bigl(1+2(a-1)p_{i}\Delta\bigr)
≤ebm​alg0+2​(a−1)​pi​Δ≤ebm​(alg0+pi​Δ)=ebm​alg.\displaystyle\leq e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}_{0}+2(a-1)p_{i}\Delta}\leq e^{b_{m}(\operatorname{alg}_{0}+p_{i}\Delta)}=e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}}.

Here we used 1+x≤ex1+x\leq e^{x}, bm≥2​(a−1)b_{m}\geq 2(a-1), and (13).

Case 2: Δ≤1/2\Delta\leq 1/2. Now alg0−alg1≥1/2\operatorname{alg}_{0}-\operatorname{alg}_{1}\geq 1/2, so alg0≥1/2\operatorname{alg}_{0}\geq 1/2 and alg−alg1≥1/2\operatorname{alg}-\operatorname{alg}_{1}\geq 1/2. For the deletion term, induction gives

𝔼⁡[aOPT0]ebm​alg≤e−(bm−bm−1)​alg0≤e−(bm−bm−1)/2=mm+1.\frac{\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{0}}]}{e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}}}\leq e^{-(b_{m}-b_{m-1})\operatorname{alg}_{0}}\leq e^{-(b_{m}-b_{m-1})/2}=\frac{m}{m+1}.

For the contraction term, using pi≤1p_{i}\leq 1 and alg1≥0\operatorname{alg}_{1}\geq 0 gives

pi​(a−1)​𝔼​[aOPT1]ebm​alg≤(a−1)e−bm​(alg−alg1)≤(a−1)e−bm/2=(a−1)​e−am+1≤1m+1.\frac{p_{i}(a-1)\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}}]}{e^{b_{m}\operatorname{alg}}}\leq(a-1)e^{-b_{m}(\operatorname{alg}-\operatorname{alg}_{1})}\leq(a-1)e^{-b_{m}/2}=\frac{(a-1)e^{-a}}{m+1}\leq\frac{1}{m+1}.

The two bounds sum to at most one, proving the induction step.

For an adversary that sees what the algorithm sees and controls the remaining part of the arrival order adaptively, define each residual alg⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}) by backward induction in the finite-horizon zero-sum game. The adversary first chooses an unseen item; after that item’s value is revealed, the algorithm chooses the better of deletion and contraction. Thus alg⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal{S}) is the minimum over (indices of) items of the right side of (13), with the corresponding guaranteed continuation values. Choose a minimizing item ii for the induction above. All its steps still hold: the unseen values remain independent with the original distributions, and the deletion continuation has value at least that of contraction. This proves the same invariant for the adversarial game.

Finally, Jensen’s inequality yields

(log⁡a)​opt≤log⁡𝔼⁡[aOPT]≤bn​alg.(\log a)\operatorname{opt}\leq\log\mathbb{E}[a^{\operatorname{OPT}}]\leq b_{n}\operatorname{alg}.

Taking a=max⁡{2,log⁡(n+1)}a=\max\{2,\log(n+1)\} makes bn=O⁡(log⁡n)b_{n}=O(\log n) and log⁡a=Θ⁡(log⁡log⁡n)\log a=\Theta(\log\log n) as nn grows. The resulting ratio is O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n), completing the proof. ∎

6 Upper Bound for the Free-Order Prophet Problem

Theorem 6.1.

Let kk be the least integer at least two such that kk≥2​n+2k^{k}\geq 2n+2. For every downward-closed instance with independent nonnegative integrable values, there is an order σ\sigma, chosen from the priors, for which

opt⁡(X)≤(25​k+2)​algσ⁡(X).\operatorname{opt}(X)\leq(25k+2)\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X).

In particular, the free-order prophet problem has competitive ratio O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)O(\log n/\log\log n).

Throughout this section the feasibility family is fixed; we write opt⁡(W)\operatorname{opt}(W) and algσ⁡(W)\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(W) to indicate which random values WW / distributions thereof are used. For a nonnegative variable WW, its excess function is

EW​(v)=𝔼⁡[(W−v)+](v≥0).E_{W}(v)=\mathbb{E}[(W-v)_{+}]\qquad(v\geq 0).

It satisfies the following basic scaling identity: Ea​W​(v)=a​EW​(v/a)E_{aW}(v)=aE_{W}(v/a) for a>0a>0. If YY is a mixture with sampling probabilities wj/Ww_{j}/W (where W=∑jwjW=\sum_{j}w_{j}) and conditional distributions YjY_{j}, then EY​(v)=∑j(wj/W)​EYj​(v)E_{Y}(v)=\sum_{j}(w_{j}/W)E_{Y_{j}}(v). We use the deletion and contraction notation from the preceding section inside continuation arguments.

6.1 Constant Bound for Activated Exponentials

An activated exponential YY of scale s>0s>0 equals an exponential variable of mean ss with probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], and zero otherwise, with independent activation. Its excess function is

EY(v)=pse−v/s.E_{Y}(v)=pse^{-v/s}.

This can be obtained by integrating the tail probability Pr(Y>z)=pe−z/s\Pr(Y>z)=pe^{-z/s} over z≥vz\geq v. The zero variable is allowed by taking p=0p=0 and any positive scale. Below we will prove a result for activated exponentials, that essentially says the free-order prophet problem admits a constant ratio restricted to activated exponential values. This motivates the reduction of the general problem to activated exponentials, which we discuss later. We use a similar comparison between recurrences as in the proof of the earlier binary-value upper bound.

Intuition.

For a feasible next item of value WW, let alg0\operatorname{alg}_{0} and alg1\operatorname{alg}_{1} be the optimal future rewards after rejecting or accepting it. Their difference is the opportunity cost of acceptance, and is nonnegative by downward closure. The online value is exactly

𝔼⁡[max⁡{alg0,W+alg1}]=alg0+EW​(alg0−alg1).\mathbb{E}[\max\{\operatorname{alg}_{0},W+\operatorname{alg}_{1}\}]=\operatorname{alg}_{0}+E_{W}(\operatorname{alg}_{0}-\operatorname{alg}_{1}). (15)

For an activated exponential, this increment has the same exponential shape that appears when comparing the two offline continuation moments. Sorting by scale ensures that both continuation moments can be compared at the current scale.

Lemma 6.2 (Decreasing-scale order).

Let Y1,…,YnY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} be independent activated exponentials with scales s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n}. If σ\sigma lists the items in nonincreasing order of sis_{i}, then opt⁡(Y)≤2​algσ⁡(Y)\operatorname{opt}(Y)\leq 2\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(Y).

Proof.

In a residual instance, let ss be its largest remaining scale, OPT\operatorname{OPT} its realized prophet benchmark, and alg\operatorname{alg} its optimal online continuation value in the inherited order. We prove by induction that

𝔼⁡[eOPT/(2​s)]≤ealg/s.\mathbb{E}[e^{\operatorname{OPT}/(2s)}]\leq e^{\operatorname{alg}/s}. (16)

An empty continuation has moment one. If a nonempty continuation has largest scale s′≤ss^{\prime}\leq s, then its inductive bound is valid also at denominator 2​s2s. Specifically, for its benchmark OPTj\operatorname{OPT}_{j} and online value algj\operatorname{alg}_{j}, concavity of z↦zs′/sz\mapsto z^{s^{\prime}/s} gives

𝔼⁡[eOPTj/(2​s)]≤(𝔼⁡[eOPTj/(2​s′)])s′/s≤ealgj/s.\mathbb{E}[e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{j}/(2s)}]\leq\bigl(\mathbb{E}[e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{j}/(2s^{\prime})}]\bigr)^{s^{\prime}/s}\leq e^{\operatorname{alg}_{j}/s}.

An empty continuation satisfies the same inequality. If the current item is infeasible, only the deletion continuation is needed.

Otherwise let YY be the current reward, whose scale is ss, and let pp be its activation probability. On the same realization of the future values, downward closure gives OPT1≤OPT0\operatorname{OPT}_{1}\leq\operatorname{OPT}_{0} and OPT=max⁡{OPT0,Y+OPT1}\operatorname{OPT}=\max\{\operatorname{OPT}_{0},Y+\operatorname{OPT}_{1}\}. Thus

eOPT/(2​s)≤eOPT0/(2​s)+(eY/(2​s)−1)​eOPT1/(2​s).e^{\operatorname{OPT}/(2s)}\leq e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{0}/(2s)}+(e^{Y/(2s)}-1)e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}/(2s)}.

To verify this inequality, the added term is nonnegative if the deletion branch wins; if the acceptance branch wins, subtract its value and use eOPT0/(2​s)≥eOPT1/(2​s)e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{0}/(2s)}\geq e^{\operatorname{OPT}_{1}/(2s)}. An exponential of mean ss has moment

∫0∞ez/(2​s)e−z/sd​zs=2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{z/(2s)}e^{-z/s}\,\frac{dz}{s}=2

at 1/(2​s)1/(2s). Consequently 𝔼⁡[eY/(2​s)−1]=p\mathbb{E}[e^{Y/(2s)}-1]=p. The current reward is independent of both continuation benchmarks, so the continuation bounds imply

𝔼⁡[eOPT/(2​s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{\operatorname{OPT}/(2s)}] ≤ealg0/s+p​ealg1/s\displaystyle\leq e^{\operatorname{alg}_{0}/s}+pe^{\operatorname{alg}_{1}/s}
=ealg0/s(1+pe−(alg0−alg1)/s)\displaystyle=e^{\operatorname{alg}_{0}/s}\bigl(1+pe^{-(\operatorname{alg}_{0}-\operatorname{alg}_{1})/s}\bigr)
≤exp⁡(alg0+pse−(alg0−alg1)/ss)=ealg/s.\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(\frac{\operatorname{alg}_{0}+pse^{-(\operatorname{alg}_{0}-\operatorname{alg}_{1})/s}}{s}\right)=e^{\operatorname{alg}/s}.

The last identity is the online recurrence (15), with EY(v)=pse−v/sE_{Y}(v)=pse^{-v/s}. This proves (16). At the initial state ℱ\mathcal{F}, Jensen’s inequality gives opt⁡(Y)/(2​s)≤log⁡𝔼⁡[eOPT/(2​s)]≤algσ⁡(Y)/s\operatorname{opt}(Y)/(2s)\leq\log\mathbb{E}[e^{\operatorname{OPT}/(2s)}]\leq\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(Y)/s. Multiplying by 2​s2s proves the lemma. ∎

6.2 The Reduction via Excess Domination

We seek a short list of activated exponential distributions Yi,jY_{i,j} for each item, and a sampling distribution DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i} on their indices. After sampling jij_{i} independently from each DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}, draw YiY_{i} from the conditional distribution Yi,jiY_{i,j_{i}}. All these choices and draws are independent across items. The algorithm observes the original values XiX_{i}, not the auxiliary draws; the auxiliaries are used merely to determine an order and serve in its analysis.

To state exactly which comparisons are required, for each item ii, write

μi=𝔼⁡[Xi]>0,Ui=min⁡{Xi/μi,2​n}.\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]>0,\qquad U_{i}=\min\{X_{i}/\mu_{i},2n\}.

The auxiliary distributions are in these normalized units. The normalization Ui=min⁡{Xi/μi,2​n}U_{i}=\min\{X_{i}/\mu_{i},2n\} ensures both Ui≤2​nU_{i}\leq 2n and 𝔼⁡[Ui]≤1\mathbb{E}[U_{i}]\leq 1. The capping is without loss of generality, since very large values can be collected by an algorithm taking the first item above its cap. Its cost is controlled in Lemma 6.3 below. The desired relations, for every v≥0v\geq 0, are

EYi,j​(v)\displaystyle E_{Y_{i,j}}(v) ≤EUi​(v)+1n\displaystyle\leq E_{U_{i}}(v)+\frac{1}{n} for every ​j,\displaystyle\text{for every }j, (17)
E(Ui−k)+​(v)\displaystyle E_{(U_{i}-k)_{+}}(v) ≤E6​k​Yi​(v)\displaystyle\leq E_{6kY_{i}}(v) in expectation over ​ji∼Diaux.\displaystyle\text{in expectation over }j_{i}\sim D^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}. (18)

Here, the cost from shifting UiU_{i} by kk is covered by preselecting a fixed feasible set of large total mean. The following lemma formally controls the costs of capping and shifting.

Lemma 6.3 (Cost of capping and shifting).

Let μi=𝔼⁡[Xi]>0\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]>0 and Ui=min⁡{Xi/μi,2​n}U_{i}=\min\{X_{i}/\mu_{i},2n\} each item ii. For every fixed order σ\sigma,

  • •

    The contribution from realized values above 2​n2n is controlled:

    ∑i𝔼⁡[(Xi−2​n​μi)+]≤2​algσ⁡(X),\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-2n\mu_{i})_{+}]\leq 2\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X), (19)
  • •

    The offset by 1/n1/n in Equation 17 is controlled:

    max⁡∑i∈SS∈ℱ⁡μi≤algσ⁡(X),1n​∑iμi≤algσ⁡(X),\max_{S\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i\in S}\mu_{i}\leq\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X),\qquad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}\leq\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X), (20)
  • •

    The cost of shifting UiU_{i} by kk is controlled:

    opt⁡(X)≤(2+k)​algσ⁡(X)+opt⁡((μi​(Ui−k)+)i).\operatorname{opt}(X)\leq(2+k)\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)+\operatorname{opt}\bigl((\mu_{i}(U_{i}-k)_{+})_{i}\bigr). (21)
Proof.

Markov’s inequality gives Pr⁡(Xi>2​n​μi)≤1/(2​n)\Pr(X_{i}>2n\mu_{i})\leq 1/(2n). Consider the algorithm that takes the first item exceeding its cap, and no other item. Every singleton under consideration is feasible. The probability that no item preceding ii exceeds its cap is at least 1/21/2, by the union bound; this event is independent of XiX_{i}. On an exceedance the policy earns at least (Xi−2​n​μi)+(X_{i}-2n\mu_{i})_{+}. Summing over the possible accepted identities gives expected reward at least half the left side of (19). The optimal online algorithm is at least as good.

An algorithm that preselects a feasible set maximizing the sum of its means proves the first bound in (20). An algorithm that preselects the single item of largest mean proves the second, since there are at most nn retained items and ∑iμi/n≤maxi⁡μi\sum_{i}\mu_{i}/n\leq\max_{i}\mu_{i}.

On every realization, capping can reduce the value of a feasible set by at most ∑i(Xi−2​n​μi)+\sum_{i}(X_{i}-2n\mu_{i})_{+}. Also

μi​Ui≤k​μi+μi​(Ui−k)+.\mu_{i}U_{i}\leq k\mu_{i}+\mu_{i}(U_{i}-k)_{+}.

Apply this inequality on each feasible set and maximize. Taking expectations, (19) and (20) yield (21). If no retained item remains, all three assertions are immediate with zero benchmark and reward. ∎

The next lemma shows that a construction satisfying these conditions implies the main theorem of this section. We will discuss the actual construction later.

Lemma 6.4 (Reduction through excess domination).

Suppose that, for every item ii, an independent auxiliary family of activated exponentials {Yi,j}\{Y_{i,j}\} and sampling distribution DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i} satisfy (17)–(18). Let si,js_{i,j} be the scale of Yi,jY_{i,j}. Independently sample the indices, sort the original items in nonincreasing order of μi​si,ji\mu_{i}s_{i,j_{i}}, and run the optimal online algorithm in that order. This policy satisfies

opt⁡(X)≤(25​k+2)​𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)].\operatorname{opt}(X)\leq(25k+2)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)].

Therefore some fixed order attains the ratio in Theorem 6.1.

Proof.

We use the bounds of Lemma 6.3 below to handle the loss from capping, shifting, and offsetting.

Conditional online comparison. Fix all sampled indices. After scaling back by μi\mu_{i}, the auxiliary rewards μi​Yi,ji\mu_{i}Y_{i,j_{i}} are independent activated exponentials, and σ\sigma is their decreasing-scale order. Scaling (17) gives

Eμi​Yi,ji​(v)≤Eμi​Ui​(v)+μin≤EXi​(v)+μin.E_{\mu_{i}Y_{i,j_{i}}}(v)\leq E_{\mu_{i}U_{i}}(v)+\frac{\mu_{i}}{n}\leq E_{X_{i}}(v)+\frac{\mu_{i}}{n}.

For this fixed order, replace one original item by its auxiliary variable. At the position replaced, the two distributions face the same future continuation values alg0≥alg1\operatorname{alg}_{0}\geq\operatorname{alg}_{1} in any residual feasible state. By (15), the replacement can increase the expected value by at most μi/n\mu_{i}/n. This uniform bound propagates to every earlier position: raising each of the two future continuation values by at most μi/n\mu_{i}/n raises their maximum by at most that amount. Backward induction therefore bounds the change in the value of the whole instance by μi/n\mu_{i}/n. Replacing all marginals successively proves

algσ⁡((μi​Yi,ji)i)≤algσ⁡(X)+1n​∑iμi.\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}\bigl((\mu_{i}Y_{i,j_{i}})_{i}\bigr)\leq\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}.

Lemma 6.2 applies conditional on these same indices {ji}\{j_{i}\}. Averaging its guarantee, and using that the conditional prophet benchmarks average to the prophet benchmark for the independent mixture distributions {Yi}\{Y_{i}\}, gives

opt⁡((μi​Yi)i)≤2​(𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)]+1n​∑iμi)≤4​𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)].\operatorname{opt}\bigl((\mu_{i}Y_{i})_{i}\bigr)\leq 2\left(\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)]+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}\right)\leq 4\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)]. (22)

The last inequality is one of the bounds in Equation 20, valid for every fixed order.

Unconditional prophet comparison. Increasing an item’s excess at every threshold can only increase the prophet benchmark. Indeed, fix all other values and write z0z_{0} for the best value without the item and z1z_{1} for the best value of other items when the item is required. Downward closure gives z0≥z1z_{0}\geq z_{1}. For a feasible item with independent reward WW, its conditional benchmark is z0+EW​(z0−z1)z_{0}+E_{W}(z_{0}-z_{1}). The claimed monotonicity follows by replacing the value distributions one at a time. Apply it to (18), scaled back to original units by μi\mu_{i}:

opt⁡((μi​(Ui−k)+)i)≤6​k​opt⁡((μi​Yi)i).\operatorname{opt}\bigl((\mu_{i}(U_{i}-k)_{+})_{i}\bigr)\leq 6k\,\operatorname{opt}\bigl((\mu_{i}Y_{i})_{i}\bigr). (23)

Independence is preserved after averaging over the sampled indices, since every item has its own independent index and conditional reward draw.

Finally Lemma 6.3 bounds the cap and the removed part below kk by (2+k)​algσ​(X)(2+k)\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X) in every order. Average that bound and combine (22) and (23) to obtain

opt⁡(X)≤(2+k)​𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)]+6​k​opt⁡((μi​Yi)i)≤(25​k+2)​𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)].\operatorname{opt}(X)\leq(2+k)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)]+6k\,\operatorname{opt}\bigl((\mu_{i}Y_{i})_{i}\bigr)\leq(25k+2)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)].

At least one of the finitely many resulting permutations has online value at least its average. Fixing that permutation proves the last assertion. ∎

6.3 Construction of Auxiliary Distributions

Now we present the actual construction of the auxiliary activated exponential variables, and show that they satisfy the desired domination conditions.

One finite grid for each normalized item.

Suppress the item index and consider 0≤U≤2​n0\leq U\leq 2n with 𝔼⁡[U]≤1\mathbb{E}[U]\leq 1. Denote its “regularized” excess by

g⁡(v)=EU​(v)+1n.g(v)=E_{U}(v)+\frac{1}{n}.

This function is nonincreasing, equals 1/n1/n for v≥2​nv\geq 2n, and satisfies 1/n≤g⁡(v)≤1+1/n≤21/n\leq g(v)\leq 1+1/n\leq 2. For any x≤vx\leq v, therefore, 1≤g⁡(x)/g⁡(v)≤n+11\leq g(x)/g(v)\leq n+1. We choose grid points xj=kjx_{j}=k^{j} for 0≤j<k0\leq j<k, such that the kk intervals [xj,xj+1)[x_{j},x_{j+1}) that cover [1,2​n)[1,2n). For notational simplicity, we also let the grid extend beyond 2​n2n, i.e., xj=kjx_{j}=k^{j} for any positive jj. The actual construction only involves up to kk intervals.

The distribution Yi,jY_{i,j} “responsible for” interval jj will be based on a decreasing exponential excess curve starting at height g⁡(xj)g(x_{j}). Recall that we need Yi,jY_{i,j} to be dominated by UiU_{i}, which means a sharp subsequent decline of gg may force the excess curve of Yi,jY_{i,j} to decay quickly. This is potentially problematic, because we also want the mixture YiY_{i} to dominate UiU_{i} after shifting and scaling. We compensate by assigning more sampling weight to that interval. The next lemma gives the construction and both required comparisons.

Lemma 6.5 (Discrete auxiliary laws).

For every 0≤U≤2​n0\leq U\leq 2n with 𝔼⁡[U]≤1\mathbb{E}[U]\leq 1, there are kk activated exponential variables YjY_{j}, with positive scales sjs_{j}, and weights wj>0w_{j}>0 such that their mixture YY, sampled with probabilities wj/Ww_{j}/W where W=∑jwjW=\sum_{j}w_{j}, satisfies, for every v≥0v\geq 0,

EYj​(v)≤EU​(v)+1nfor each ​j,E(U−k)+​(v)≤E6​k​Y​(v).E_{Y_{j}}(v)\leq E_{U}(v)+\frac{1}{n}\quad\text{for each }j,\qquad E_{(U-k)_{+}}(v)\leq E_{6kY}(v).

All distributions YjY_{j} and weights wjw_{j} depend only on the distribution of UU and on nn.

Proof.

Use the regularized excess gg and the grid x0,…,xkx_{0},\dots,x_{k} as defined above. Write gj=g⁡(xj)g_{j}=g(x_{j}) for each interval jj. For 0≤j<k0\leq j<k, set

λj=supz≥xjlog⁡(gj/g⁡(z))z,Fj​(v)=gj​e−λj​v,wj=(gjgj+2)1/k.\lambda_{j}=\sup_{z\geq x_{j}}\frac{\log(g_{j}/g(z))}{z},\qquad F_{j}(v)=g_{j}e^{-\lambda_{j}v},\qquad w_{j}=\left(\frac{g_{j}}{g_{j+2}}\right)^{1/k}. (24)

FjF_{j} is an auxiliary function that simplifies presentation. The rates λj\lambda_{j} are finite because z≥xj≥1z\geq x_{j}\geq 1 and gj/g⁡(z)≤n+1g_{j}/g(z)\leq n+1. If gj>1/ng_{j}>1/n, evaluation at z=2​nz=2n also shows λj>0\lambda_{j}>0. If gj=1/ng_{j}=1/n, then U≤xjU\leq x_{j} almost surely; set Yj=0Y_{j}=0 and sj=1s_{j}=1. In all other cases set

sj=1/λj,pj=λj​gj​e−λj,s_{j}=1/\lambda_{j},\qquad p_{j}=\lambda_{j}g_{j}e^{-\lambda_{j}}, (25)

and let YjY_{j} be an exponential of mean sjs_{j} activated with probability pjp_{j}. We sample the interval with probability wj/Ww_{j}/W.

Each conditional distribution YjY_{j} is dominated. For v≤xjv\leq x_{j}, monotonicity gives Fj​(v)≤gj≤g⁡(v)F_{j}(v)\leq g_{j}\leq g(v). For v≥xjv\geq x_{j}, the definition of λj\lambda_{j} gives λj​v≥log⁡(gj/g⁡(v))\lambda_{j}v\geq\log(g_{j}/g(v)), hence Fj​(v)≤g​(v)F_{j}(v)\leq g(v) again. It remains to ensure that this curve is an actual activated-exponential excess function. Matching Fj​(v)F_{j}(v) without a shift would require activation probability λj​gj\lambda_{j}g_{j}, which need not be at most one. Instead, (25) gives

pj≤2​λj​e−λj≤2/e<1,EYj​(v)=Fj​(v+1)≤Fj​(v)≤g⁡(v).p_{j}\leq 2\lambda_{j}e^{-\lambda_{j}}\leq 2/e<1,\qquad E_{Y_{j}}(v)=F_{j}(v+1)\leq F_{j}(v)\leq g(v).

Here z​e−z≤1/eze^{-z}\leq 1/e for z≥0z\geq 0. Thus the one-unit shift changes the initial height just enough to guarantee a valid probability, without changing the decay rate.

One interval pays for a target threshold. Fix t∈[1,2​n)t\in[1,2n), and let jj satisfy xj≤t<xj+1x_{j}\leq t<x_{j+1}. We claim

wj​Fj​(t/k)≥12​g​(t).w_{j}F_{j}(t/k)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}g(t). (26)

For each z≥xjz\geq x_{j} contributing to the supremum in (24), consider the corresponding decay factor

(gjg⁡(z))t/(k​z).\left(\frac{g_{j}}{g(z)}\right)^{t/(kz)}.

There are three ranges. If xj≤z≤tx_{j}\leq z\leq t, then t/(k​z)≤1t/(kz)\leq 1 and g⁡(z)≥g⁡(t)g(z)\geq g(t), so the factor is at most gj/g⁡(t)g_{j}/g(t). If t≤z≤xj+2t\leq z\leq x_{j+2}, the exponent is at most 1/k1/k, and the factor is at most (gj/gj+2)1/k=wj(g_{j}/g_{j+2})^{1/k}=w_{j}. Finally, if z≥xj+2z\geq x_{j+2}, then z≥k​tz\geq kt and the exponent is at most 1/k21/k^{2}. Even the full possible decline of gg, n+1n+1, costs at most

(n+1)1/k2≤k1/k≤2.(n+1)^{1/k^{2}}\leq k^{1/k}\leq 2.

The first inequality uses n+1≤kkn+1\leq k^{k}, and the last follows from k≤2kk\leq 2^{k} for integers k≥2k\geq 2. Since wj≥1w_{j}\geq 1 and gj/g⁡(t)≥1g_{j}/g(t)\geq 1, every factor in all three ranges is at most 2​wj​gj/g⁡(t)2w_{j}g_{j}/g(t). Taking the supremum gives eλj​t/k≤2​wj​gj/g⁡(t)e^{\lambda_{j}t/k}\leq 2w_{j}g_{j}/g(t), which is exactly (26).

The weights have total at most 3​k3k. Multiplying the even-indexed weights telescopes:

w0w2⋯w2​a=(g0g2g2g4⋯g2​ag2​a+2)1/k≤(n+1)1/k≤k.w_{0}w_{2}\cdots w_{2a}=\left(\frac{g_{0}}{g_{2}}\frac{g_{2}}{g_{4}}\cdots\frac{g_{2a}}{g_{2a+2}}\right)^{1/k}\leq(n+1)^{1/k}\leq k.

Here, a=⌊(k−1)/2⌋a=\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor. The same holds for the odd-indexed weights, and for an empty product the bound is immediate. Since every wj≥1w_{j}\geq 1, expanding the product within one parity gives

∏jwj=∏j(1+(wj−1))≥1+∑j(wj−1).\prod_{j}w_{j}=\prod_{j}(1+(w_{j}-1))\geq 1+\sum_{j}(w_{j}-1).

Each parity therefore adds at most k−1k-1 above weight one per interval. There are at most kk intervals, so W≤k+2​(k−1)≤3​kW\leq k+2(k-1)\leq 3k.

The scaled mixture 6​k​Y6kY covers the shifted marginal. For any v≥0v\geq 0, put t=v+kt=v+k. If EU​(t)=0E_{U}(t)=0, the desired inequality is immediate. Otherwise k≤t<2​nk\leq t<2n, so tt lies in a retained interval jj with gj>1/ng_{j}>1/n. Its associated distribution YjY_{j} is nonzero, and

EYj​(v/k)=Fj​(v/k+1)=Fj​(t/k).E_{Y_{j}}(v/k)=F_{j}(v/k+1)=F_{j}(t/k).

Keep this one interval in the mixture and use (26) and W≤3​kW\leq 3k:

EY​(v/k)≥wjW​Fj​(t/k)≥g⁡(t)2​W≥EU​(t)6​k.E_{Y}(v/k)\geq\frac{w_{j}}{W}F_{j}(t/k)\geq\frac{g(t)}{2W}\geq\frac{E_{U}(t)}{6k}.

Because excess is nonincreasing in its threshold,

E6​k​Y​(v)=6​k​EY​(v/(6​k))≥6​k​EY​(v/k)≥EU​(v+k)=E(U−k)+​(v).E_{6kY}(v)=6kE_{Y}\bigl(v/(6k)\bigr)\geq 6kE_{Y}(v/k)\geq E_{U}(v+k)=E_{(U-k)_{+}}(v).

This proves the second comparison and completes the lemma. ∎

Remark.

The same parameter kk pays for two quantities: the grid has at most kk intervals, and each alternating product of compensating weights is at most kk. A target threshold t∈[xj,xj+1)t\in[x_{j},x_{j+1}) in the regularized excess function gg needs only its own interval’s (i.e., YjY_{j}’s) contribution. The construction does not require an approximation by one exponential simultaneously at all target thresholds.

Now we are ready to prove the main theorem of the section.

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

Apply Lemma 6.5 independently to every normalized capped variable UiU_{i}, using its weights to define DiauxD^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}. The resulting distributions satisfy (17) and (18). Lemma 6.4 then gives opt⁡(X)≤(25​k+2)​𝔼σ​[algσ⁡(X)]\operatorname{opt}(X)\leq(25k+2)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\operatorname{alg}_{\sigma}(X)] and hence the stated guarantee for some fixed order. For k>2k>2, minimality gives (k−1)​log⁡(k−1)<log⁡(2​n+2)≤k​log⁡k(k-1)\log(k-1)<\log(2n+2)\leq k\log k; these inequalities imply k=Θ⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)k=\Theta(\log n/\log\log n) as nn grows. This proves the asserted asymptotic ratio. ∎

AI Disclosure

The author interacted with GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 extensively and adaptively in the process of obtaining the results. All proofs were digested, verified, simplified, and reinterpreted by the author. In particular, the layered self-encoding interpretation, the earliest divergence formulation in the lower bound for the standard prophet problem, and the harvesting game in the lower bound for the prophet secretary problem are human. The author also persistently instructed GPT-6 to find a discrete construction of the upper bound for the free-order prophet problem, which is (in the author’s opinion) significantly cleaner than the continuous sampling argument initially found. The author used GPT-6 to assist in writing, mostly in the main technical sections. All sections were verified and polished by the author, who takes full responsibility of all contents.
